process.title: Login or session handling of [name] can be bypassed or brute-forced
process.desc: Weak authentication — no limit on login attempts, sessions that never expire, guessable tokens or a flawed password-reset flow — lets attackers log in as real users.
controls: Use a proven identity provider or framework instead of custom login code
Rate-limit and monitor failed logins
Short-lived sessions, rotated on login and privilege change
Secure, single-use password-reset tokens

process.title: Forged or tampered tokens accepted by [name]
process.desc: Tokens (JWT, SAML, API keys) are accepted without fully checking the signature, signing key, issuer, audience and expiry, so attackers can mint their own tokens.
controls: Validate signature with an allow-list of algorithms and keys
Check issuer, audience, expiry and not-before on every request
Rotate signing keys and keep them in a vault/HSM
process.example: Storm-0558 (2023): a stolen Microsoft consumer signing key was accepted for enterprise tokens because of a validation flaw, giving access to email at about 25 organizations.

process.title: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) against [name]
process.desc: The browser automatically sends the user's cookies, so a malicious site can make a signed-in user's browser perform actions (change email, transfer money) without their intent.
controls: SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies
Anti-CSRF tokens for state-changing requests
Check the Origin header; never change state on GET

process.title: Unauthenticated callers reach [name]
process.desc: A component that handles sensitive data or is business-critical accepts requests that are not authenticated, so anyone who can reach it can use it.
controls: Authenticate every inbound request (OAuth2/OIDC, mTLS between services)
Deny by default at the gateway
Inventory endpoints so test or legacy APIs are not left open
process.example: Optus (2022): a customer API reachable from the internet without authentication — attributed by the regulator to an access-control coding error — exposed data of about 9.8 million people.

process.title: Injection (SQL, NoSQL, OS command, template) in [name]
process.desc: User-controlled input is built into a query, command or template, letting an attacker read or change data or run commands with the service's rights.
controls: Parameterised queries / ORM; never concatenate input
Avoid shell calls; pass arguments as arrays
Allow-list validation on input
Least-privilege database and OS accounts
process.example: MOVEit Transfer (2023, CVE-2023-34362): an unauthenticated SQL injection was used for mass data theft from thousands of organizations.

process.title: Mass assignment lets users change protected fields
process.desc: The API binds the whole request body to an object, so a user can set fields they should not control — role, price, owner, verification status.
controls: Explicit allow-lists (DTOs) for writable fields
Separate read and write models
Server-side authorization per field

process.title: Race conditions in business transactions
process.desc: Concurrent requests exploit check-then-act gaps: a coupon used twice, a balance withdrawn twice, stock oversold.
controls: Database transactions with row locks or atomic updates
Idempotency keys on payment and order APIs
Unique constraints for one-time actions

process.title: Path traversal or malicious file upload
process.desc: File names like ../../etc/passwd or uploaded scripts let attackers read or overwrite files, or run code on the server.
controls: Generate server-side file names; never use user paths
Store uploads outside the web root, on separate storage
Check type by content, limit size, scan for malware

process.title: Data from third-party APIs is trusted without validation
process.desc: Responses from partners or external APIs are used as if they were safe — following their redirects, storing their HTML, passing their values into queries.
controls: Validate and sanitise third-party data like user input
Use TLS and verify certificates for outgoing calls
Timeouts and limits on responses; do not follow redirects blindly

process.title: Compromised dependency or build pipeline ships malicious code in [name]
process.desc: A malicious package, a hijacked maintainer account or a tampered build system inserts a backdoor into what you deploy, signed as your own software.
controls: Pin dependency versions and verify checksums/signatures
Protect CI/CD: least-privilege tokens, protected branches, reviewed pipeline changes
SBOM, dependency scanning, private package mirror
process.example: SolarWinds (2020): attackers modified the build system so that signed Orion updates contained the SUNBURST backdoor. xz Utils (2024, CVE-2024-3094): a backdoor inserted by a co-maintainer who had built trust over about two years.

process.title: Security events in [name] are not logged
process.desc: Logins, failed access checks, permission changes and access to sensitive records are not recorded with who, what, when and from where, so misuse cannot be detected or proven.
controls: Log security events with user, action, target, time and source IP
Ship logs to a central store the service cannot modify
Alert on suspicious patterns (many failures, privilege changes)

process.title: Log injection forges or hides log entries
process.desc: User input is written to logs unchanged, so newlines and control characters create fake entries or break log parsing and alerting.
controls: Structured (JSON) logging
Encode or strip control characters from logged values

process.title: An attacker on [name] can delete or alter its logs
process.desc: Logs are only stored where the compromised service or host can modify them, so the first thing an attacker does is erase their tracks.
controls: Forward logs in real time to a separate, append-only store
Alert when log forwarding stops

process.title: Broken object-level authorization (IDOR) in [name]
process.desc: The service returns or changes a record when the caller supplies its ID, without checking that the caller is allowed to access that particular record.
controls: Check ownership/permission for every object access, server-side
Use unguessable IDs as defence in depth (not as the control)
Automated tests that request other users' objects
process.example: First American Financial (2019): changing a number in a document URL exposed about 885 million mortgage records without any login.

process.title: API responses expose more data than the client needs
process.desc: Endpoints return full objects (internal IDs, emails, flags, other users' fields) and rely on the front-end to hide them.
controls: Explicit response schemas per endpoint
Never return internal or other users' fields
Review API responses in code review and tests

process.title: Secrets hard-coded in code, scripts, images or config of [name]
process.desc: Passwords, API keys and private keys committed to repositories or baked into images and scripts can be read by anyone with access to those artefacts.
controls: Keep secrets in a vault/secret manager and inject at runtime
Secret scanning in CI and on repositories
Rotate any secret that was ever committed
process.example: Uber (2022): an attacker found admin credentials for the company's privileged-access system in a PowerShell script on a network share. Toyota (2022): an access key sat in a public GitHub repository for about five years.

process.title: Sensitive data written to logs, traces or diagnostic files
process.desc: Tokens, passwords, personal data or full request bodies end up in logs, traces, crash reports or support uploads, which many more people and systems can read.
controls: Redact secrets and personal data before logging
Never log Authorization headers, cookies or full bodies
Restrict and expire access to logs and diagnostic files
process.example: Okta (2023): HAR files uploaded to the support system contained session tokens that attackers used to hijack customer sessions.

process.title: Error messages reveal internal details
process.desc: Stack traces, SQL errors and version strings in responses give attackers a map of the system for further attacks.
controls: Generic error responses to clients; details only in server logs
Disable debug mode in production

process.title: Personalised responses cached and served to other users
process.desc: A CDN or reverse proxy caches pages or API responses that contain one user's data and serves them to others.
controls: Cache-Control: private/no-store on personalised responses
Cache keys that include the user or vary correctly
Test caching rules after CDN changes
process.example: Steam (December 2015): a caching misconfiguration during a traffic spike showed users other people's account pages.

process.title: Secrets exposed in crash dumps or memory snapshots
process.desc: Keys and tokens held in memory end up in core dumps, heap snapshots or debug captures that are copied to less-protected environments.
controls: Keep signing keys in an HSM or managed key service
Disable or scrub crash dumps in production
Treat debug environments as sensitive
process.example: Storm-0558 (2023): the stolen signing key had ended up in a crash dump that was moved to a debugging environment.

process.title: Unrestricted resource consumption in [name]
process.desc: Missing limits on request rate, payload size, page size or expensive operations let one client exhaust CPU, memory, connections or paid third-party quotas.
controls: Rate limits and quotas per client
Limits on payload, page and batch sizes
Timeouts and bounded worker pools

process.title: Small requests trigger very expensive work (ReDoS, decompression bombs)
process.desc: Crafted input makes a regular expression, parser or decompressor do enormous amounts of work, pinning the CPU or filling memory.
controls: Linear-time regex engines or timeouts
Limits on decompressed size and nesting depth
Input length limits

process.title: Attackers run up the cloud or third-party bill of [name]
process.desc: Autoscaling, serverless functions and paid APIs (SMS, email, AI models) keep serving abusive traffic, turning an attack into a large invoice.
controls: Budgets and billing alerts
Per-user quotas on paid actions (SMS, AI calls)
Caps on autoscaling

process.title: Missing function-level authorization in [name]
process.desc: Administrative or privileged functions are reachable by normal users because the check is only done in the UI or not at all.
controls: Deny by default; central authorization for every endpoint
Separate admin APIs and tests that call them as a normal user

process.title: Server-side request forgery (SSRF) in [name]
process.desc: The service fetches URLs chosen by the user, so attackers make it call internal systems or the cloud metadata endpoint with its network position and credentials.
controls: Allow-list destinations; block private and metadata IP ranges
Use a separate egress proxy
Require IMDSv2 / metadata protection on cloud hosts
process.example: Capital One (2019): SSRF via a misconfigured WAF reached the EC2 metadata service, whose over-privileged role could read S3 buckets with data on about 100 million people.

process.title: Known-vulnerable component allows remote code execution in [name]
process.desc: An unpatched framework, library or server with a public exploit lets attackers run code inside the service.
controls: Dependency and image scanning with a patch SLA
Inventory of components (SBOM)
WAF/virtual patching while updating
process.example: Equifax (2017): an unpatched Apache Struts flaw (CVE-2017-5638). Log4Shell (2021, CVE-2021-44228): remote code execution through a logging library.

process.title: Insecure deserialization of untrusted data
process.desc: Turning untrusted bytes into native objects can execute code or bypass checks.
controls: Never deserialize untrusted native objects; use JSON with schema validation
Allow-list types if native formats are unavoidable

process.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS) in [name]
process.desc: Untrusted content is rendered as HTML or script, so attackers run code in other users' browsers with their session.
controls: Context-aware output encoding; framework auto-escaping
Content-Security-Policy
HttpOnly cookies

process.title: Compromise of [name] gives administrator control
process.desc: The component runs with administrative or root rights, so any code-execution flaw becomes full control of the host.
controls: Run as a dedicated least-privileged account
Drop capabilities; read-only file system; containers/sandboxing

process.title: Over-privileged service identity of [name]
process.desc: The cloud role, service account or database user used by the service can do far more than it needs, so one flaw exposes everything that identity can reach.
controls: Least-privilege roles per service, reviewed regularly
Separate identities per environment and function
Alert on unusual use of service identities
process.example: Capital One (2019): the role available to the compromised server could list and read many S3 buckets.

process.title: Crown jewel [name] is reachable from a less-trusted zone
process.desc: A business-critical component accepts traffic that crosses a trust boundary, so it is directly exposed to attacks from that zone.
controls: Put a gateway or proxy in front and expose only needed operations
Strict input validation and authorization at the boundary
Network segmentation

process.title: Prompt injection changes what [name] does
process.desc: Instructions hidden in user input, documents, web pages or emails processed by the model override the system prompt, making it ignore rules, leak data or misuse its tools.
controls: Treat all model input as untrusted; keep instructions and data separate
Least-privilege tools and human approval for impactful actions
Filter and monitor outputs; red-team with injection test sets

process.title: [name] reveals sensitive data from prompts, context or training data
process.desc: The model repeats personal data, secrets or other users' content from its context window, retrieved documents or fine-tuning data.
controls: Do not put secrets in prompts or context
Per-user authorization on retrieved documents (RAG)
Redact personal data before indexing or fine-tuning

process.title: Excessive agency: [name] takes harmful actions through its tools
process.desc: An LLM agent can call APIs, run code, send email or change data with broad permissions, so a manipulated or mistaken model acts with those rights.
controls: Give tools the minimum permissions and scope
Require confirmation for state-changing actions
Rate-limit and log every tool call

process.title: Model output from [name] used unsafely (XSS, SQL, shell)
process.desc: Text generated by the model is inserted into web pages, queries or commands without validation, turning prompt injection into classic injection.
controls: Encode model output for its destination; never execute it directly
Validate against schemas for structured output

process.title: System prompt of [name] can be extracted
process.desc: Users can make the model reveal its hidden instructions, exposing business rules, filters and any credentials or internal details placed there.
controls: Assume the system prompt is public; keep secrets and authorization logic out of it
Enforce rules outside the model
process.example: Bing Chat (February 2023): users made the assistant reveal its confidential instructions and internal code name.

process.title: Unbounded model usage makes [name] slow or expensive
process.desc: Long prompts, large outputs or automated querying consume GPU capacity and paid tokens, causing outages or large bills.
controls: Per-user quotas, input/output token limits and timeouts
Budget alerts on model usage

process.title: Price or amount in [name] can be changed by the client
process.desc: The server trusts price, discount, currency or quantity values sent by the browser or app, so users pay less than they should.
controls: Recalculate amounts server-side from the catalogue/order
Sign or look up amounts when calling the payment provider

process.title: Card data processed by [name] leaks into logs or storage
process.desc: Full card numbers or CVV end up in logs, analytics, error reports or the database, bringing the whole system into PCI DSS scope and exposing cardholder data.
controls: Use the payment provider's hosted fields/tokenisation so card data never touches your servers
Mask card numbers in logs; never store CVV

process.title: Card testing (carding) through [name]
process.desc: Fraudsters use the checkout to test large numbers of stolen cards with small payments, causing chargebacks, fees and provider sanctions.
controls: Bot detection and rate limits on payment attempts
3-D Secure / risk scoring from the provider
Alert on spikes in declined payments

process.title: Deeply nested or batched GraphQL queries overload [name]
process.desc: A single query with deep nesting, aliases or batching makes the server resolve millions of fields.
controls: Query depth, complexity and cost limits
Limit batching and aliases; persisted queries for public clients

process.title: GraphQL introspection exposes the full schema of [name]
process.desc: Introspection and field suggestions reveal every type, field and mutation, including internal and unfinished ones.
controls: Disable introspection and field suggestions in production
Authorization on every field and mutation, not only on the endpoint

process.title: CORS policy of [name] lets other websites read responses
process.desc: Reflecting any Origin, or allowing "null" or wildcard origins together with credentials, lets a malicious site read signed-in users' data.
controls: Explicit allow-list of origins
Never combine Access-Control-Allow-Credentials with wildcard or reflected origins

process.title: Open redirect in [name] used for phishing or token theft
process.desc: A redirect parameter accepts any URL, so links on your trusted domain send users to attacker sites or leak OAuth codes.
controls: Allow-list redirect targets or use relative paths only
Exact redirect URI matching for OAuth

process.title: Clickjacking against [name]
process.desc: The site can be framed by another page that tricks users into clicking buttons (approve, delete, transfer) they cannot see.
controls: Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors (or X-Frame-Options)
Confirmation for sensitive actions

process.title: OAuth/OIDC flow of [name] lets attackers steal codes or tokens
process.desc: Loose redirect URI matching, missing state/PKCE or the implicit flow let attackers intercept authorization codes or tokens.
controls: Exact redirect URI matching; PKCE for all clients
Validate state/nonce; no implicit flow
Short-lived, audience-restricted tokens

process.title: Forged SAML assertions accepted by [name]
process.desc: Unsigned assertions, signature-wrapping flaws or a stolen token-signing certificate let attackers log in as anyone.
controls: Validate signatures with a maintained library; reject unsigned assertions
Protect and monitor the token-signing certificate (HSM)
Alert on logins without matching IdP events
process.example: SolarWinds campaign (2020): attackers forged SAML tokens ("Golden SAML") with a stolen signing certificate to access cloud email.

process.title: Poisoned pipeline execution in [name]
process.desc: Pull requests, build scripts or third-party actions run attacker-controlled code inside the pipeline, which has access to secrets and deployment rights.
controls: Do not run untrusted pull requests with secrets
Pin third-party actions to commit SHAs
Separate build and deploy permissions
process.example: tj-actions/changed-files (2025, CVE-2025-30066): a compromised GitHub Action dumped CI secrets into build logs of thousands of repositories.

process.title: Secrets in [name] exposed through logs, forks or over-scoped tokens
process.desc: Pipeline secrets are printed to logs, available to forked builds, or are long-lived tokens with broad scopes.
controls: Short-lived OIDC credentials instead of stored cloud keys
Mask secrets in logs; scope tokens per job
Rotate secrets after incidents
process.example: CircleCI (2023): malware on an engineer's laptop stole an MFA-backed session; customers had to rotate all secrets stored in the platform.

process.title: Dependency confusion or typosquatting pulls malicious packages into [name]
process.desc: Package managers fetch a public package with the same or a similar name as an internal one, running attacker code during the build.
controls: Scoped/namespaced internal packages and a single private registry
Lock files with integrity hashes
Block install scripts where possible
process.example: Dependency confusion (2021): a researcher got code executed inside dozens of large companies, including Apple and Microsoft, by publishing public packages named like their internal ones.

process.title: Event injection into [name]
process.desc: Functions triggered by queues, storage uploads or webhooks trust event content (file names, metadata, message bodies) that attackers can control.
controls: Validate every event field like user input
Restrict who can publish events or upload files that trigger functions

process.title: Poison messages crash [name] repeatedly
process.desc: A malformed or oversized message makes the consumer fail, get redelivered and fail again, blocking all following messages.
controls: Dead-letter queues with retry limits
Schema validation and size limits before processing

process.title: Emails can be sent pretending to come from your domain
process.desc: Without SPF, DKIM and an enforcing DMARC policy, attackers send phishing or fake invoices that appear to come from you.
controls: SPF and DKIM for all sending services
DMARC with p=reject after monitoring

process.title: Email header injection through [name]
process.desc: User input placed in email headers (subject, to, reply-to) adds recipients or rewrites messages sent from your system.
controls: Strip CR/LF from header values; use a mail library API instead of raw headers

process.title: Administrative actions in [name] are not separately audited
process.desc: Changes made through admin functions (role changes, refunds, data exports, configuration) are not recorded with before/after values and who approved them.
controls: Dedicated audit trail for admin actions with old and new values
Four-eyes approval for the most critical actions

process.title: Users can deny transactions made through [name]
process.desc: Orders, payments or approvals are accepted without a reliable record of who confirmed them and when.
controls: Store who, what, when and from where for each transaction
Explicit confirmation step and receipts for important transactions

process.title: Requests through [name] cannot be traced across services
process.desc: Without correlation IDs passed between services, an investigation cannot follow one user action through the system.
controls: Generate and propagate a request/trace ID; log it everywhere
Central log search across services

process.title: Unsynchronised clocks make the timeline of [name] unreliable
process.desc: Servers without time synchronisation write timestamps that do not line up, so the order of events in an incident cannot be proven.
controls: NTP on all hosts; log in UTC with time zone
Monitor clock drift

process.title: Container of [name] runs as root or privileged
process.desc: Root or privileged containers, host mounts or added capabilities turn an application flaw into control of the node.
controls: Run as non-root with a read-only root file system
Drop all capabilities; no privileged mode or host mounts
Pod security standards (restricted)

process.title: Unverified or outdated base image for [name]
process.desc: Images built from unpinned public base images inherit known vulnerabilities or a tampered upstream image.
controls: Pin base images by digest; rebuild regularly
Scan images and verify signatures before deploy

process.title: Secrets for [name] in plain environment variables or baked into the image
process.desc: Environment variables and image layers are visible to anyone who can inspect the container, read crash dumps or pull the image.
controls: Mount secrets from a secret store at runtime
Never copy secrets into image layers; scan images for secrets

process.title: Admin portal [name] reachable from the internet
process.desc: Administrative interfaces exposed publicly are constantly attacked with stolen credentials and exploits.
controls: Restrict admin access to VPN / zero-trust access or allow-listed networks
Separate admin application from the public site

process.title: Sensitive admin actions in [name] without re-authentication
process.desc: A stolen or unattended admin session can change roles, export data or disable controls without being asked to prove identity again.
controls: Step-up authentication (MFA) for sensitive actions
Short admin session lifetimes

process.title: [name] trusts the mobile app to enforce rules
process.desc: Limits, prices and permissions are only checked in the app, so a modified app or direct API calls bypass them.
controls: Enforce every rule on the server
Treat the app like any other untrusted client

process.title: Old app versions keep using deprecated endpoints of [name]
process.desc: Legacy API versions stay online for old app installs and miss security fixes applied to the current version.
controls: Inventory and retire old API versions
Minimum supported app version enforced by the backend

process.title: Unsupported runtime or operating system under [name]
process.desc: End-of-life frameworks, runtimes or OS versions no longer receive security patches.
controls: Track end-of-life dates; upgrade plan per component
Isolate legacy systems that cannot be upgraded

process.title: Edge rules or functions for [name] changed through a compromised account
process.desc: Whoever controls the CDN configuration can redirect traffic, inject scripts or disable protection for the whole site.
controls: MFA and least privilege on CDN accounts; change approval
Alert on configuration changes

process.title: Function [name] hits concurrency limits
process.desc: Bursts of events use up account-wide concurrency, so this and unrelated functions are throttled.
controls: Reserved concurrency per critical function
Queue and back-pressure in front of functions

process.title: Batched GraphQL queries bypass login rate limits in [name]
process.desc: Aliases or batching let one HTTP request try hundreds of passwords or one-time codes, slipping past per-request rate limits.
controls: Rate-limit by operation, not by request
Disallow batching for authentication mutations

process.title: Messages processed twice or out of order by [name]
process.desc: At-least-once delivery without idempotency creates duplicate orders or payments; out-of-order processing applies old state.
controls: Idempotency keys and de-duplication
Version numbers or sequence checks on state changes

process.title: [name] abused to send spam
process.desc: Contact, invite or password-reset forms send email to any address, so attackers use your domain to spam until it is blocklisted.
controls: Rate limits and CAPTCHA on forms that send email
Do not include user-supplied text in automatic emails

process.title: Huge or numerous uploads exhaust storage of [name]
process.desc: Uploads without size and count limits fill disks or storage quotas.
controls: Per-user quotas and maximum file size
Stream to object storage instead of local disk

process.title: Uploaded files served by [name] run scripts in your domain
process.desc: HTML or SVG uploads served from the application's own domain execute JavaScript in users' sessions (stored XSS).
controls: Serve user files from a separate domain
Content-Disposition: attachment and correct content types
Sanitise or convert SVG/HTML

process.title: Payment status in [name] taken from the browser instead of the provider
process.desc: The order is marked as paid because of a success redirect or URL parameter, which a user can fake.
controls: Confirm payment server-to-server or via signed provider webhooks
Check amount and currency against the order

process.title: Account enumeration through login, reset or sign-up of [name]
process.desc: Different messages or timings reveal which emails or usernames have accounts, feeding phishing and credential stuffing.
controls: Identical responses and timing for existing and unknown accounts
Rate limits on these endpoints

process.title: Notifications from [name] reveal sensitive content on lock screens
process.desc: Push notifications include codes, balances or medical/personal details visible without unlocking the phone.
controls: Keep notification text generic; show details inside the app
Never send one-time codes with full context in notifications

process.title: Configuration or code of [name] writable by its own service account
process.desc: If the running service can modify its own binaries or config, any code-execution flaw becomes persistent.
controls: Separate deploy and runtime accounts; read-only application files
Integrity monitoring on config files

process.title: Disk full on the host stops [name]
process.desc: Logs, temporary files or uploads fill the disk and the service crashes or stops writing data.
controls: Log rotation and quotas; separate data volumes
Disk-usage alerts

process.title: Private API responses for [name] cached at the edge
process.desc: Responses that depend on the user are cached by the CDN and served to other users.
controls: Cache-Control: private/no-store on authenticated responses
Cache only explicitly public paths

process.title: Cache-busting requests bypass the CDN for [name]
process.desc: Random query strings or headers force every request through to the origin, defeating the CDN during an attack.
controls: Normalise or ignore unknown query parameters in the cache key
Rate limiting at the edge

process.title: One shared static credential lets anything impersonate [name] towards other services
process.desc: [name] calls other services with a long-lived key or password that is copied into several places. Whoever obtains it can act as [name], and nobody can tell the calls apart.
controls: Give each service its own workload identity (managed identity, SPIFFE, mTLS certificates)
Short-lived tokens issued per call or per session
Rotate and scope any remaining static secrets

process.title: [name] hangs or fails when a dependency is slow or down
process.desc: Calls from [name] have no timeouts, retries with back-off or circuit breakers, so one slow database or partner API exhausts its threads and takes it down too.
controls: Timeouts on every outgoing call
Circuit breakers and bulkheads per dependency
Graceful degradation and cached fallbacks for non-critical data

process.title: Business rules of [name] enforced only in the client
process.desc: Limits, prices, workflow steps or permissions are checked in the browser or app but not again in [name], so a modified request skips them.
controls: Re-validate every rule on the server
Treat client-side checks as usability only
Test with an intercepting proxy (e.g. ZAP, Burp) as part of QA

process.title: Requests from external entities to [name] are logged without the user behind them
process.desc: Logs record the endpoint and status but not which authenticated user or client made the request, so suspicious actions cannot be attributed.
controls: Log the authenticated subject, client ID and source IP with each security-relevant action
Propagate a correlation ID to downstream services
Protect logs from modification

process.title: Configuration file [name] exposes secrets
process.desc: .env, YAML or JSON configuration holds database passwords, cloud keys or API tokens and ends up readable — served by the web server, committed to git, baked into an image or attached to a ticket.
controls: Keep secrets in a secrets manager and reference them, not in config files
Block dotfiles and config paths at the web server
Secret scanning in repositories and images
Rotate any secret that was ever in a config file
process.example: Exposed .env files (2024): an extortion campaign reported by Palo Alto Unit 42 scanned about 230 million targets for public .env files, harvested over 1,100 AWS keys and other tokens, and ransomed data from cloud storage.

process.title: Changing [name] changes security behaviour
process.desc: Whoever can edit the configuration can point the application at another endpoint, switch off authentication or TLS checks, or enable debug features — no code change needed.
controls: Read-only configuration at runtime; changes only through review and deployment
Integrity monitoring or signed configuration
Separate high-risk settings (auth, TLS, endpoints) and alert on their change

process.title: A bad configuration change in [name] takes services down
process.desc: A typo, wrong value or untested change is pushed everywhere at once and breaks every instance that reads it.
controls: Validate configuration (schema, test environment) before release
Staged roll-out with automatic rollback
Keep the last known-good configuration available

process.title: Insecure defaults left in [name]
process.desc: Debug mode, sample accounts, default passwords or open admin consoles from the default configuration are still enabled in production.
controls: Hardened baseline configuration (e.g. CIS Benchmarks)
Configuration scanning in the pipeline
Remove samples and default accounts on install

process.title: Private keys controlling [name] stolen
process.desc: Whoever holds the signing keys (or enough of the validator or multisig keys) can move funds or write to the ledger, and transactions cannot be reversed.
controls: Keys in HSMs or MPC wallets, never on ordinary servers
Threshold signing with independent operators; remove stale delegated signers
Withdrawal limits and time delays for large transfers
process.example: Ronin Network (2022): attackers obtained five of the nine validator keys — including one delegated permission that was never revoked — and withdrew about $625 million.

process.title: Smart contract flaw lets attackers drain or alter [name]
process.desc: Logic or access-control bugs (reentrancy, unchecked callers, price-oracle manipulation) in deployed contracts are exploited, and the code cannot simply be patched.
controls: Independent audits and formal verification of contracts
Pause / circuit-breaker functions with multisig control
Bug bounty and on-chain monitoring of unusual calls
process.example: Poly Network (2021): a flaw in a cross-chain contract call let an attacker replace the trusted keeper and take about $610 million (most was later returned).

process.title: Data copied to [name] leaves the building unencrypted
process.desc: USB sticks, SD cards and external drives are small, often unencrypted and easily lost or taken out of the building.
controls: Enforce encryption on removable media (e.g. BitLocker To Go)
Allow only approved devices; block mass storage where not needed
DLP rules for copying sensitive data

process.title: Malware spreads through [name]
process.desc: Infected media runs malware when it is plugged in or a file on it is opened, and can bridge networks that are otherwise isolated.
controls: Disable autorun; scan media on insertion
Block execution from removable drives
Dedicated, scanned transfer stations for isolated networks
process.example: Raspberry Robin (2022): a worm spread through infected USB drives with a malicious shortcut file; Microsoft found it on devices in almost 1,000 organisations and linked it to later ransomware.

process.title: Data on [name] readable after loss, decommissioning or snapshotting
process.desc: A disk that leaves its machine — returned, sold, recycled, or copied as a snapshot — still holds readable data if it was not encrypted or wiped.
controls: Full-disk encryption with keys in a TPM or KMS
Certified wiping (NIST SP 800-88) or destruction before disposal
Encrypted snapshots with restricted sharing

process.title: Disk failure or a wiper destroys [name]
process.desc: A failing drive, a corrupted file system or wiper malware deletes the data, and the newest usable copy is old or missing.
controls: Redundancy (RAID, replication) plus independent backups
Disk health monitoring
Restore tests

process.title: Malicious update of a third-party package used by [name]
process.desc: A maintainer account is taken over, a maintainer turns malicious, or a lookalike package is published — and the next build of [name] pulls in the backdoor.
controls: Pin versions and verify checksums (lock files)
Delay adoption of brand-new versions; review diffs of critical dependencies
Private mirror with malware scanning
Track dependencies with an SBOM
process.example: xz utils (2024, CVE-2024-3094): a contributor who had gained maintainer trust over two years hid a backdoor targeting SSH servers in release tarballs; it was caught shortly before reaching stable Linux distributions.

process.title: Plugin or extension runs with the full rights of [name]
process.desc: Plugins are loaded into the same process without isolation, so a vulnerable or malicious plugin can do anything the host application can.
controls: Allow only reviewed plugins from trusted sources
Isolate plugins (separate process, sandbox, restricted APIs)
Keep plugins updated and remove unused ones

process.title: Scheduled job [name] runs attacker-controlled code with high rights
process.desc: The job runs as root or a service admin, and its script, schedule or working directory can be changed by others — an easy path to persistence and privilege escalation.
controls: Run jobs with a dedicated low-privilege account
Scripts and schedules writable only by administrators
Monitor changes to cron, systemd timers and scheduled tasks

process.title: Runs and failures of [name] are not recorded
process.desc: There is no record of when the job ran, with which input and what it changed, and failures are silent.
controls: Log start, end, inputs and result of every run
Heartbeat monitoring that alerts when a run is missed or fails
Keep run history

process.title: Overlapping or runaway runs of [name] exhaust resources
process.desc: A run takes longer than its interval, so runs pile up; or a bad input makes one run loop for hours and block everything else.
controls: Locking so only one run is active
Timeouts and resource limits per run
Back-pressure on input volume

process.title: Input files or records for [name] can be planted
process.desc: Batch jobs pick up whatever is in a shared folder, bucket or staging table, so anyone who can write there controls what is processed.
controls: Restrict who can write to the input location
Validate and authenticate input (checksums, signatures, schema)
Quarantine and reject unexpected files

process.title: Untrusted model files run code when [name] loads them
process.desc: Common model formats (Python pickle in PyTorch .pt/.bin, some Keras files) can execute code on load. Downloading a model from a public hub is running someone else's program.
controls: Prefer safe formats (safetensors, ONNX) and refuse pickle from untrusted sources
Scan models before use; pin by hash
Load models in a sandbox without credentials or network
process.example: Hugging Face (2024): JFrog found about 100 models on the hub with malicious payloads, including ones that opened a reverse shell as soon as the PyTorch file was loaded.

process.title: Cluster or notebook API of [name] runs jobs for anyone who can reach it
process.desc: Distributed compute frameworks and notebooks (Ray, Jupyter, MLflow) often ship without authentication; anyone on the network can submit code.
controls: Never expose these services to the internet; put them behind authenticated access
Enable built-in authentication where it exists
Network policies limiting who can reach the dashboard and job APIs
process.example: ShadowRay (2024): attackers used the unauthenticated Ray Jobs API (CVE-2023-48022, disputed by the vendor) to take over hundreds of AI clusters, steal credentials and run cryptominers.

process.title: GPU memory of [name] leaks data between users or jobs
process.desc: Memory on shared GPUs is not always cleared between processes, so one tenant can read another tenant's model responses or data.
controls: Dedicated GPUs or strong isolation (MIG, VMs) for sensitive workloads
Apply driver and firmware updates
Do not mix trusted and untrusted jobs on one GPU
process.example: LeftoverLocals (2024, CVE-2023-4969): Trail of Bits showed that leftover GPU local memory on several vendors' GPUs let one process reconstruct another user's LLM responses.

process.title: Training or fine-tuning data for [name] poisoned
process.desc: Manipulated training data plants a backdoor or bias in the model, which then behaves normally except on the attacker's trigger.
controls: Control and record where training data comes from
Validate and de-duplicate datasets; look for outliers
Evaluate models against known triggers before release

process.title: Cryptominers or runaway jobs consume [name]
process.desc: Expensive GPU capacity is hijacked for mining or burned by unbounded jobs, causing outages for real work and large bills.
controls: Quotas and budgets with alerts
Monitor GPU utilisation per job and owner
Restrict who can submit jobs

process.title: Model weights or datasets on [name] copied out
process.desc: Weights, checkpoints and training sets are valuable intellectual property and often contain personal data, but are stored in buckets and shared volumes with broad access.
controls: Access control and encryption for model and dataset storage
Egress controls and download monitoring
Treat training data under the same rules as production data

process.title: Users break out of kiosk [name] to the operating system
process.desc: Print dialogs, help links, file pickers or keyboard shortcuts let a user leave the kiosk application and reach the desktop, a shell or the network.
controls: Use the platform's assigned-access / kiosk mode
Disable shortcuts, dialogs and external links
Least-privilege local account; no network access beyond what is needed

process.title: Session or data of the previous user remains on [name]
process.desc: The next person at the shared terminal sees, or continues, the previous user's session, documents or form data.
controls: Automatic sign-out after inactivity and at session end
Wipe browser data and files between sessions
Clear visual cue when a session is still active

process.title: Skimmers, USB devices or overlays added to [name]
process.desc: Unattended terminals are physically tampered with: card skimmers, keyloggers, rogue USB devices or fake screens.
controls: Tamper-evident enclosures and seals; regular inspection
Disable unused ports
Alert on device changes and reboots

process.title: Infostealer on [name] steals saved passwords and session cookies
process.desc: Malware from cracked software, fake updates or malicious ads copies browser passwords and session cookies, which are sold and used to log in to company systems — often from a personal or unmanaged device.
controls: Managed devices with EDR for access to company systems
Phishing-resistant MFA and short session lifetimes; bind sessions to the device
Do not allow saving work passwords in browsers; use a password manager

process.title: Users are local administrators on [name]
process.desc: With local admin rights, any malware the user runs can disable protection, install drivers and dump credentials.
controls: Remove standing local admin rights; use just-in-time elevation
Application allow-listing for privileged tools
Unique local admin passwords (e.g. Windows LAPS)

process.title: Malicious macros, extensions or downloads run on [name]
process.desc: Office macros, browser extensions and downloaded tools run with the user's rights and change files, settings or browser sessions.
controls: Block macros from the internet; allow only signed macros
Allow-list browser extensions
Attack-surface-reduction rules and EDR

process.title: Code changes to [name] merged without review
process.desc: One person can change production code alone, so a malicious or mistaken change cannot be attributed to a deliberate decision.
controls: Protected branches with required review
Signed commits
Separate approver for releases

process.title: Command injection through arguments or variables in [name]
process.desc: File names, user input or environment values are expanded unquoted in shell or PowerShell commands, so a crafted value runs extra commands.
controls: Quote all variables; avoid eval and string-built commands
Use a real programming language with argument arrays for anything non-trivial
Lint scripts (ShellCheck, PSScriptAnalyzer)

process.title: Script [name] runs with high rights from a location others can write
process.desc: An administrator or scheduler runs the script, but the script file, the folder or a tool it calls can be modified by ordinary users.
controls: Store privileged scripts in admin-only locations
Use absolute paths; do not trust PATH or the working directory
Sign scripts and enforce signature checks

process.title: [name] downloads and runs code without checking it
process.desc: Patterns like curl | bash or Invoke-Expression on a downloaded string run whatever the server returns at that moment.
controls: Download, verify checksum or signature, then run
Pin versions of downloaded tools
Host internal copies of third-party scripts

process.title: Who ran [name] and with which arguments is not logged
process.desc: Scripts run by people or tools leave no record, so misuse cannot be investigated.
controls: Enable script block / command logging (e.g. PowerShell logging)
Run privileged scripts through a tool that records the operator
Send logs to central storage

process.title: Test environment [name] has weaker sign-in but reaches production
process.desc: Test and legacy environments skip MFA and monitoring, yet hold accounts, apps or credentials with rights in production.
controls: Same identity controls (MFA, conditional access) for non-production
No production permissions from test tenants, apps or accounts
Inventory and decommission legacy test environments
process.example: Microsoft (2024): Midnight Blizzard password-sprayed a legacy non-production test tenant account without MFA, then abused a test OAuth app to read corporate mailboxes.

process.title: Real customer data copied into [name]
process.desc: Production data is copied to test so that tests are realistic, but test has broader access, weaker logging and more people.
controls: Synthetic or masked data for test
If real data is unavoidable, the same controls as production
Automatic expiry of test copies

process.title: Debug features left enabled in [name]
process.desc: Debug endpoints, verbose errors, heap-dump or actuator endpoints and test backdoors expose internals and secrets.
controls: Disable debug features in builds that leave the developer machine
Block management endpoints at the gateway
Scan for debug endpoints before release

process.title: Shared credentials or network paths connect [name] to production
process.desc: The same service accounts, keys or open network routes are used in test and production, so compromising the weaker environment gives the stronger one.
controls: Separate accounts, keys and cloud subscriptions per environment
No network routes from test to production
Different secrets per environment

process.title: Stolen OAuth tokens of [name] used to pull your data
process.desc: Integrations hold long-lived OAuth or API tokens for your SaaS systems. When the integration vendor is breached, the attacker uses those tokens directly — no password or MFA involved.
controls: Inventory connected apps and their scopes; remove unused ones
Restrict tokens by IP and lifetime where possible
Monitor API exports by integrations; be ready to revoke all tokens quickly
process.example: Salesloft Drift (2025): attackers used stolen OAuth tokens of the Drift integration to export data from many companies' Salesforce instances and search it for further credentials.

process.title: Integration [name] has broader scopes than it uses
process.desc: Connectors are granted admin or full-access scopes during set-up "to make it work", so a flaw in the connector reaches everything.
controls: Grant the narrowest scopes; review them at each change
Dedicated integration accounts per connector
Periodic access review of non-human identities

process.title: Data passed by [name] between systems is not validated
process.desc: The connector maps fields from one system to another and trusts both sides, carrying injected or malformed data into systems that assume it was checked.
controls: Validate against the target system's schema and rules
Reject and quarantine unexpected values
Encode data for the target context

process.title: Actions by [name] appear as a generic service account
process.desc: Everything the integration does is logged as one technical user, so you cannot tell which person or triggering event caused a change.
controls: Pass and log the originating user or event ID
One service identity per integration
Keep integration run logs

process.title: [name] fails silently and data stops syncing
process.desc: Expired credentials, API changes or rate limits stop the integration, and nobody notices until records are missing.
controls: Health checks and alerts on sync lag
Dead-letter queues and retry with back-off
Credential expiry monitoring

process.title: Monitoring tool [name] exposes data-source credentials and internals
process.desc: Dashboards hold credentials for databases and cloud accounts, and show architecture details; an exposed or vulnerable instance gives all of that away.
controls: Never expose monitoring tools to the internet; require SSO
Patch promptly — these tools are actively targeted
Read-only, least-privilege data-source credentials
process.example: Grafana (CVE-2021-43798): an unauthenticated path traversal let attackers read files such as grafana.ini and the Grafana database from self-hosted servers; CISA lists it as exploited.

process.title: Attackers silence alerts or change thresholds in [name]
process.desc: An attacker with access to the monitoring system mutes alerts, deletes rules or raises thresholds before acting.
controls: Alert on changes to alert rules and notification channels
Separate admin rights for monitoring configuration
Monitor the monitoring (dead-man's switch)

process.title: Monitoring agents of [name] run as root and accept remote commands
process.desc: Agents installed on every host run with full rights and can execute actions pushed from the central server — a compromise of the server is a compromise of every host.
controls: Disable remote command features you do not use
Restrict and audit who can push actions
Run agents with minimal rights where supported

process.title: Alert floods or an outage of [name] hide real incidents
process.desc: Too many noisy alerts, or the monitoring system being down, mean a real attack or outage is not seen in time.
controls: Tune alerts; route by severity
Redundant monitoring for critical signals
External uptime checks

process.title: Data warehouse [name] reachable with stolen passwords and no MFA
process.desc: Analytics platforms hold copies of everything, are reachable from the internet, and are often accessed with long-lived passwords without MFA or network restrictions.
controls: Enforce MFA or key-pair / SSO authentication for every user
Network policies limiting access to known locations
Rotate and expire credentials; alert on bulk exports
process.example: Snowflake customers (2024): attackers used credentials stolen by infostealer malware to log in to over 100 customer accounts that had no MFA, and stole large datasets for extortion.

process.title: Analysts can query personal data in [name] they do not need
process.desc: Raw personal data is loaded into the warehouse and everyone with access can query it, far beyond the original purpose.
controls: Pseudonymise or mask personal data on load
Row- and column-level security
Purpose-based access reviews

process.title: Pipelines into [name] load wrong or manipulated data
process.desc: A compromised or buggy source feeds bad data, and reports and decisions — or ML models — are built on it.
controls: Data-quality checks and anomaly detection on load
Track lineage of each dataset
Restrict who can write to raw zones

process.title: Runaway queries in [name] exhaust capacity or budget
process.desc: A single heavy query or a loop in a dashboard uses all credits or slots and blocks other users.
controls: Resource monitors, quotas and budgets
Query timeouts
Separate compute for heavy workloads

process.title: Security product [name] itself is exploited
process.desc: Security tools run with the highest privileges and sit at network edges, so a flaw in them gives an attacker exactly the position they want.
controls: Patch security products as fast as anything internet-facing
Restrict their management interfaces
Include them in vulnerability scanning and monitoring

process.title: Attackers disable or reconfigure [name]
process.desc: Attackers who gain admin rights turn off protection, add exclusions or change policies before deploying malware.
controls: Tamper protection; changes only with separate admin approval
Alert when protection is disabled or exclusions are added
Separate admin accounts for security tools

process.title: A faulty update of [name] takes down the systems it protects
process.desc: Security software updates itself automatically and runs deep in the system; one bad update can crash every machine at once.
controls: Staged roll-out of agent and content updates where the vendor allows
Tested recovery procedures (boot media, recovery keys available)
Ask vendors how updates are tested and staged
process.example: CrowdStrike (July 2024): a faulty content update for the Falcon sensor crashed about 8.5 million Windows machines, halting airlines, hospitals and banks.

process.title: Alerts from [name] are not reviewed or kept
process.desc: The control detects suspicious activity, but nobody looks at the alerts and they expire before an incident is investigated.
controls: Route alerts to a monitored queue with an owner
Retain alerts and events long enough to investigate
Measure time to triage

process.title: [name] is readable without authentication or encryption
process.desc: The component is marked as open: anyone who can reach it, or listen to the network, can read its data.
controls: Require authentication for every access
Encrypt in transit and at rest
Restrict network access to known clients

process.title: Anyone can change data in [name]
process.desc: Without authentication and integrity protection, any reachable client can write or alter data.
controls: Authenticated, authorised writes only
Integrity checks (signatures, checksums) on stored data
Audit writes

process.title: Biometric data in [name] leaks — and cannot be changed
process.desc: Fingerprints and face templates are permanent: once leaked, they cannot be reset like a password. Many systems also store them unencrypted next to names and access rights.
controls: Store templates encrypted and separately from identities; prefer on-device matching
Never store raw images when templates suffice
Strict access control and data-protection impact assessment
process.example: Suprema BioStar 2 (2019): researchers found an unprotected database with over a million fingerprint records, face images and unencrypted passwords used by building access systems.

process.title: A fake fingerprint, photo or mask fools [name]
process.desc: Presentation attacks — printed photos, video replays, silicone fingers, deepfake video — are accepted as the real person.
controls: Liveness / presentation-attack detection tested to ISO/IEC 30107-3
Combine biometrics with a device or PIN for high-risk actions
Monitor and rate-limit failed attempts

process.title: Biometric reader [name] fails with no fallback
process.desc: When the reader or matching service is down, people are locked out — or staff prop doors open.
controls: Defined fallback (card + PIN) with the same assurance
Monitor reader health
Spare devices for critical doors

process.title: Ransomware on [name] encrypts everything it can reach
process.desc: Malicious code running on this component encrypts its data and every share and backup reachable with its credentials.
controls: Least-privilege access to shares and backups
Immutable backups
EDR with ransomware protection; segment the network

process.title: Attacker-controlled [name] exfiltrates data
process.desc: A compromised or malicious component sends data out through allowed channels (HTTPS, DNS, cloud storage).
controls: Egress filtering and proxying
DLP and anomaly detection on outbound volumes
Alert on new destinations

process.title: Documents in [name] carry hidden data
process.desc: Metadata, tracked changes, comments, hidden sheets and "redactions" that are only black boxes reveal information that was meant to be removed.
controls: Strip metadata and hidden content before sharing externally
Use real redaction tools
Export to a flat format for publication

process.title: Malicious documents opened or parsed by [name] run code
process.desc: Office files, PDFs and archives exploit macros or flaws in viewers and parsers to run code.
controls: Block macros from the internet; protected view
Convert or sandbox documents from outside (CDR)
Keep viewers and parsing libraries patched
process.example: Follina (2022, CVE-2022-30190): malicious Word documents ran code through the Windows support diagnostic tool URL handler, even with macros disabled.

process.title: XML external entities in uploaded documents read files on [name]
process.desc: Office files (.docx, .xlsx) and SVGs are XML; parsing them with external entities enabled lets an attacker read server files or reach internal URLs.
controls: Disable DTDs and external entities in all XML parsers
Use maintained libraries for office formats
Process uploads in an isolated service

process.title: Health records in [name] exposed
process.desc: Health data is among the most sensitive and valuable data. It is targeted for extortion and protected by special laws (HIPAA, GDPR special categories).
controls: MFA on every remote and administrative access
Encryption and strict role-based access
Network segmentation of clinical systems
process.example: Change Healthcare (2024): attackers entered through a remote-access portal without MFA, stole health data of about 190 million people and disrupted US claims processing for weeks.

process.title: Clinical data in [name] altered
process.desc: Changed allergies, doses or results can directly harm patients and may go unnoticed.
controls: Audit trail of every change with who and why
Signed or versioned clinical records
Plausibility checks on critical values

process.title: Access to patient records in [name] is not logged
process.desc: Health regulations require that every access is attributable; without it, snooping by staff cannot be detected.
controls: Log every read and change of a record
Break-the-glass access with justification and review
Regular access reviews

process.title: Outage of [name] stops patient care
process.desc: Ransomware or a failure makes health records unavailable to clinicians when they need them.
controls: Downtime procedures and read-only copies
Immutable backups with tested restores
Segment clinical systems from office IT

process.title: Installer or update of [name] replaced with a trojanised version
process.desc: The build or update server is compromised and ships a signed, malicious version to every customer.
controls: Secure build environment; reproducible builds
Code signing with keys in an HSM
Updates that verify signatures and pin the signing certificate
process.example: 3CX (2023): the company's signed desktop app installers were trojanised through a supply-chain compromise that itself began with a trojanised third-party application.

process.title: DLL search-order hijacking when [name] starts
process.desc: The program loads libraries from its own folder or the working directory, so a planted DLL runs with its rights.
controls: Load libraries by full path; use SetDefaultDllDirectories
Install into protected program folders
Sign and verify loaded modules

process.title: Unsigned [name] cannot be told apart from a lookalike
process.desc: Without code signing, users and endpoint protection cannot tell the real program from a malicious copy with the same name and icon.
controls: Sign every executable and installer
Publish checksums
Distribute only through official channels

process.title: Secrets extracted from [name] by reverse engineering
process.desc: API keys, passwords and endpoints compiled into the program are easy to extract.
controls: No secrets in client binaries; use per-user tokens
Server-side checks for everything the client is trusted with

process.title: Vulnerable plugin in [name] gives remote code execution
process.desc: CMS plugins and themes are the most common way in: one outdated plugin with a file-upload or injection flaw lets attackers run code on the server.
controls: Install few, well-maintained plugins; remove unused ones
Automatic security updates
Web application firewall with virtual patching
process.example: WordPress File Manager (2020, CVE-2020-25213): an unauthenticated upload flaw in a plugin installed on about 700,000 sites was mass-exploited before a patch was available.

process.title: Admin login of [name] brute-forced
process.desc: Login pages and XML-RPC endpoints are hammered with password guesses.
controls: MFA for all editors and admins
Limit login attempts; disable XML-RPC if unused
Admin area only from known networks or SSO

process.title: Pages of [name] defaced or injected with spam or skimmers
process.desc: Attackers with access insert hidden spam links, redirects or card-skimming scripts that run in visitors' browsers.
controls: File-integrity monitoring of themes and plugins
Content Security Policy
Least-privilege editor roles

process.title: User lists, backups or config files exposed by [name]
process.desc: Default REST endpoints list user names, and backup or config copies (wp-config.php.bak, database dumps) sit in the web root.
controls: Restrict user-listing endpoints
Keep backups outside the web root
Block access to config and backup file patterns

process.title: Card skimmer injected into the checkout of [name]
process.desc: Attackers change a script on the payment page (often a third-party script) and copy card details as customers type them (Magecart).
controls: Content Security Policy and Subresource Integrity on payment pages
Inventory and monitor every script on payment pages (PCI DSS 4.0 req. 6.4.3, 11.6.1)
Use a hosted payment page or iframe from the payment provider
process.example: British Airways (2018): attackers modified a script on the airline's payment page and captured card details of about 400,000 customers; the UK regulator fined the airline £20 million.

process.title: Scalper bots buy up stock in [name]
process.desc: Limited items are bought or reserved by bots within seconds, crowding out customers and overloading checkout.
controls: Purchase limits and queueing
Bot detection on add-to-cart and checkout
Verified accounts for high-demand drops

process.title: Coupons, gift cards or loyalty points in [name] abused
process.desc: Discount codes are guessed or reused, gift cards are cracked by enumeration, and loyalty points are stolen or farmed.
controls: Unguessable codes; limit attempts
One-time and per-customer limits enforced on the server
Fraud monitoring on redemptions

process.title: Customer accounts of [name] taken over to use stored cards and points
process.desc: Stolen or stuffed credentials give access to saved payment methods, addresses and loyalty balances.
controls: MFA or step-up for purchases with stored cards and address changes
Breached-password checks
Notify customers of new devices and changes

process.title: Default or shared credentials on [name]
process.desc: Devices, appliances and platforms shipped with default admin passwords — or one password shared across many devices — are taken over by automated scanning.
controls: Change defaults at install; unique credentials per device
Disable unused services (telnet, default admin UI)
process.example: Mirai (2016): malware logged into hundreds of thousands of IoT devices with default passwords and used them for record DDoS attacks.

process.title: Firewall or security group rules on [name] opened too widely
process.desc: "Temporary" allow-any rules or 0.0.0.0/0 exposures remain in place long after they were needed.
controls: Rule review and expiry dates; least-open rules
Automated checks for wide-open rules

process.title: Configuration changes on [name] are not tracked
process.desc: Network device or appliance configs are changed without versioning, so nobody can tell who opened a rule or when.
controls: Configuration backups with diffs and change tickets
Syslog of configuration commands to a central store

process.title: [name] can be abused to amplify DDoS attacks
process.desc: Open UDP services (DNS resolvers, NTP, memcached) answer spoofed requests with much larger responses aimed at a victim.
controls: Do not expose UDP services to the internet; disable recursion for public DNS
Source address validation (BCP 38)
process.example: GitHub (2018): a 1.35 Tbps attack used publicly exposed memcached servers as amplifiers.

process.title: Cloud instance credentials of [name] stolen via the metadata service
process.desc: Code running on the host — or an SSRF flaw — reads temporary cloud credentials from the instance metadata endpoint.
controls: Require IMDSv2 / metadata protection
Least-privilege instance roles
Block metadata access from containers that do not need it
process.example: Capital One (2019): credentials from the EC2 metadata service were used to read S3 data.

process.title: Long-lived cloud access keys for [name] leak
process.desc: Static access keys in laptops, CI systems or repositories are copied and used from anywhere.
controls: Short-lived role-based credentials (SSO, workload identity)
Key age alerts and automatic rotation
Secret scanning

process.title: Cloud control-plane activity for [name] not logged
process.desc: API activity logs (e.g. CloudTrail / Activity Log) are disabled, short-lived or writable by the admins they record.
controls: Organisation-wide control-plane logging to a separate account
Alert when logging is changed

process.title: DNS for [name] hijacked through the registrar or DNS provider account
process.desc: Taking over the DNS or registrar account lets attackers point your domains at their servers and obtain valid certificates.
controls: MFA and restricted access on registrar/DNS accounts; registry lock
Monitor DNS record changes and certificate issuance (CT logs)

process.title: Dangling DNS records allow subdomain takeover
process.desc: Records still point at deleted cloud resources (apps, buckets, CDN endpoints), which attackers can claim to serve content on your subdomain.
controls: Remove DNS records when resources are deleted
Scan for dangling CNAMEs regularly

process.title: One credential can read every secret in [name]
process.desc: Applications or CI jobs use broad tokens, so compromising one of them exposes all secrets in the store.
controls: Per-application policies limited to their own secrets
Short-lived authentication (workload identity) instead of static tokens

process.title: Access to secrets in [name] is not audited
process.desc: Reads and changes of secrets are not logged, so a leaked token's use cannot be traced.
controls: Enable audit devices/logs; alert on unusual reads
Retain secret-access logs centrally

process.title: Secrets store [name] unavailable stops all services
process.desc: If the store is down or sealed after a restart, every service that needs a secret fails to start.
controls: High-availability setup and tested unseal procedure
Short-lived caching of secrets in services

process.title: Logs in [name] contain personal data and are widely accessible
process.desc: Many engineers, tools and vendors can read logs that include user identifiers, IP addresses or request bodies.
controls: Minimise and pseudonymise logged personal data
Role-based access and retention limits for logs

process.title: Log flooding hides attacks or overloads [name]
process.desc: Attackers generate huge volumes of log events so real alerts are lost, storage fills up or the logging budget is exhausted.
controls: Rate-limit and sample noisy events
Alert on sudden log volume changes

process.title: Audit records in [name] can be rewritten by the people they record
process.desc: Administrators or the application can update or delete audit and transaction records, so evidence can be removed.
controls: Append-only / write-once storage for audit data
Separate ownership of audit logs from system administration

process.title: Cache poisoning in [name]
process.desc: Attackers get malicious or wrong values stored in a cache that other users or services then trust.
controls: Include all relevant inputs in cache keys
Validate data before caching; short TTLs for user-influenced data

process.title: Sessions or tokens in [name] readable without authentication
process.desc: Caches inside the network often run without passwords or TLS, so anyone who reaches them can read sessions and cached data.
controls: Enable authentication and TLS on the cache

Track where copies of the data go

Regularly test restores

Disk and queue-depth alerts

controls: Per-topic read permissions; separate topics for sensitive data

datastore.title: Ransomware encrypts files on [name]

controls: Review and remove broad permissions
Data-owner approval for access

Separate tenants in vector stores

Pass end-user identity into audit columns

Archive to cheaper immutable storage

Avoid embedding sensitive fields

Short-lived caching of secrets in services

datastore.title: Database [name] uses default or shared admin credentials

controls: Malware scanning on shares
Read-only shares where users only consume content

Reject unknown fields

Audit and alert on direct changes to payment tables

Separate credentials for the backup system

Per-client credentials limited to the minimum (insert-only, one table, one prefix)
Validate schemas and content on arrival

Review access when components are added

Document where copies go and how long they are kept

Bug bounty and on-chain monitoring of unusual calls

DLP rules for copying sensitive data

Measure time to triage

Track and close findings quickly

datastore.desc: Health regulations require that every access is attributable; without it, snooping by staff cannot be detected.
controls: Log every read and change of a record
Break-the-glass access with justification and review
Regular access reviews

datastore.title: Outage of [name] stops patient care
datastore.desc: Ransomware or a failure makes health records unavailable to clinicians when they need them.
controls: Downtime procedures and read-only copies
Immutable backups with tested restores
Segment clinical systems from office IT

datastore.title: Disk snapshots or images of [name] shared publicly
datastore.desc: Snapshots, AMIs or images are made public or shared with other accounts, exposing their full disk contents.
controls: Block public sharing at account level
Encrypt snapshots with customer-managed keys

datastore.title: Source repository [name] exposes code and secrets
datastore.desc: Repositories hold source code, infrastructure definitions and — too often — credentials in their history. A leaked token or a repository made public by mistake gives all of it away.
controls: Secret scanning with push protection; rotate anything found
SSO and MFA for the code platform; fine-grained, expiring tokens
Alert on visibility changes and mass clones

datastore.title: History or protected branches of [name] rewritten
datastore.desc: Without branch protection, anyone with write access can force-push, delete tags or merge unreviewed code into the branch that is deployed.
controls: Protected branches: no force-push, required reviews and status checks
Signed commits and tags
Mirror or back up repositories

datastore.title: Changes to repository settings of [name] are not audited
datastore.desc: Who added a deploy key, changed branch rules or invited an outside collaborator cannot be traced.
controls: Stream the code platform's audit log to central logging
Alert on new deploy keys, webhooks and admins

datastore.title: Directory [name] can be read by any account or anonymously
datastore.desc: LDAP or directory queries list all users, groups, service accounts and attributes, giving attackers a map of who to target.
controls: Disable anonymous binds; restrict read access to sensitive attributes
Monitor large directory queries (e.g. BloodHound-style enumeration)
Keep secrets out of description fields

datastore.title: Group memberships or roles in [name] changed to grant access
datastore.desc: Adding an account to a privileged group or role is a quiet way to gain or keep access.
controls: Alert on changes to privileged groups and roles
Privileged access management with approval
Regular access recertification

datastore.title: Changes to identities in [name] are not audited
datastore.desc: Account creation, password resets and role changes are not logged or not kept.
controls: Directory audit logging forwarded to central storage
Retain long enough for investigations

datastore.title: Persistent volumes of [name] readable by other workloads
datastore.desc: Shared volumes or storage classes let other pods or tenants mount the same data.
controls: One volume per workload; access modes and storage policies
Encrypt volumes
Network and RBAC rules for storage APIs

datastore.title: Images in registry [name] overwritten under the same tag
datastore.desc: Mutable tags like :latest can be replaced, so a deployment silently pulls a different image than the one that was tested.
controls: Immutable tags; deploy by digest
Sign images and verify on admission
Restrict push rights to the pipeline

datastore.title: Access to biometric data in [name] is not audited
datastore.desc: Nobody can tell who read or exported the biometric templates, so misuse or a leak cannot be investigated.
controls: Log every read, export and deletion of biometric records
Alert on bulk access
Restrict access to a small, named group

datastore.title: Sync jobs overwrite data in [name] with stale or wrong values
datastore.desc: Two-way integrations and connectors write back into the store without conflict handling, silently replacing correct data or amplifying a bad change made elsewhere.
controls: Define which system owns each field
Conflict detection (versions, timestamps) on write-back
Change history so overwritten values can be restored

interactor.title: Phishing steals [name]'s credentials or session
interactor.desc: Fake login pages — including adversary-in-the-middle kits that relay one-time codes — capture passwords and session cookies.
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys)
Short sessions; bind sessions to device
User reporting of phishing

interactor.title: Privileged account of [name] taken over (no MFA)
interactor.desc: A privileged user signs in with a password only, so one leaked or guessed password gives an attacker administrative access.
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA for all privileged and remote access
Privileged access workstations / just-in-time admin rights
interactor.example: Change Healthcare (2024): attackers used stolen credentials on a remote-access portal that did not require MFA. Colonial Pipeline (2021): access was reportedly through a VPN account without MFA.

interactor.title: MFA fatigue: [name] approves a push prompt they did not start
interactor.desc: Attackers with a stolen password send repeated push notifications (often while posing as IT support) until the user accepts one.
controls: Number matching or FIDO2 instead of simple push approval
Limit and alert on repeated MFA prompts
interactor.example: Uber (2022): a contractor accepted a push after being flooded with prompts and contacted by the attacker posing as IT.

interactor.title: Credential stuffing with passwords leaked elsewhere
interactor.desc: Attackers try username/password pairs from other breaches or infostealer logs at scale; reused passwords let them in.
controls: MFA
Breached-password checks
Rate limiting and bot detection on login
interactor.example: Snowflake customer accounts (2024): attackers used credentials from infostealer malware against accounts without MFA and stole data from many companies.

interactor.title: Account recovery or SMS codes used to take over [name]'s account
interactor.desc: Weak password-reset flows, guessable security questions or SIM-swap attacks on SMS codes give attackers control of the account.
controls: Strong reset tokens and notification on reset
Avoid SMS as the only second factor
Extra verification for recovery of privileged accounts

interactor.title: API keys or tokens of [name] stolen and reused
interactor.desc: A partner's or client app's credentials leak (code, logs, device) and attackers call your API as that client.
controls: Short-lived tokens (OAuth2 client credentials) instead of static keys
Bind keys to IP or mTLS certificate; per-client scopes
Monitor and rotate keys

interactor.title: Supplier or partner [name] used as a way in
interactor.desc: Attackers compromise a vendor with access to your systems and use that trusted connection.
controls: Least-privilege, monitored vendor access
Separate network segment for third-party access
MFA and time-limited accounts for vendors
interactor.example: Target (2013): attackers entered with credentials stolen from a refrigeration/HVAC contractor and reached payment systems.

interactor.title: Bots pose as real users of [name] (fake sign-ups, scraping, enumeration)
interactor.desc: Anonymous access lets automated clients create fake accounts, scrape data or test which emails and phone numbers are registered.
controls: Rate limits and bot detection
Same response for existing and non-existing accounts
Protect sensitive business flows (sign-up, checkout)

interactor.title: Administrative access by [name] is exposed to the internet
interactor.desc: A privileged user reaches admin functions across a trust boundary without a VPN or zero-trust gateway, so the admin login is open to the whole internet.
controls: VPN or zero-trust access for admin interfaces
Admin endpoints on a separate host/network
MFA and IP restrictions

interactor.title: Actions by [name] cannot be attributed
interactor.desc: Connections from this entity are not authenticated, so the system cannot prove who performed an action.
controls: Authenticate connections
Record user, client and request IDs in audit logs

interactor.title: Shared accounts make actions by [name] untraceable
interactor.desc: Several people use the same account, so it is impossible to tell who did what.
controls: Personal accounts only; no shared credentials
Privileged access management with individual check-out

interactor.title: [name] disputes a transaction and there is no proof
interactor.desc: A customer or partner denies placing an order, approving a payment or receiving data, and the system has no reliable evidence.
controls: Signed receipts or confirmations for important transactions
Tamper-evident transaction logs with timestamps

interactor.title: Malware on [name]'s device steals sessions or data
