interactor.desc: Infostealers and keyloggers on user or administrator devices capture passwords, session cookies and files.
controls: Managed, hardened devices for privileged users
Short sessions bound to device; re-authentication for sensitive actions
Endpoint detection and response
interactor.example: LastPass (2022): attackers installed a keylogger on a DevOps engineer's home computer via vulnerable third-party software and used the captured password to reach vault backups.

interactor.title: Insider misuse of [name]'s legitimate access
interactor.desc: Employees, support staff or administrators look up or export data they have access to but no business reason to see.
controls: Least privilege and need-to-know access
Audit and review access to sensitive records
Just-in-time access for support

interactor.title: Sensitive data left on shared or lost devices of [name]
interactor.desc: Cached pages, downloads and tokens in browser or app storage stay on shared, lost or stolen devices.
controls: Cache-Control: no-store for sensitive pages
Keep tokens out of local storage; short sessions
Device encryption / mobile app data protection

interactor.title: Help desk tricked into resetting [name]'s password or MFA
interactor.desc: An attacker calls or messages support pretending to be the user and gets the password or MFA device reset.
controls: Strong identity verification for resets (call-back, manager approval, ID check)
Extra scrutiny for privileged accounts; notify the user on reset
interactor.example: MGM Resorts (2023): attackers impersonated an employee in a call to the IT help desk and gained access that led to a major outage.

interactor.title: Consent phishing: [name] authorises a malicious app
interactor.desc: Users are tricked into granting a third-party OAuth app access to their mail or files, giving attackers long-lived tokens without a password.
controls: Admin approval for third-party app consent
Review and revoke risky app grants

interactor.title: Secrets extracted from the [name] app
interactor.desc: API keys, tokens or endpoints embedded in the app binary are recovered by decompiling it.
controls: No long-lived secrets in apps; per-user tokens from the backend
App attestation for backend calls

interactor.title: Modified app or emulator impersonates the official [name] client
interactor.desc: Repackaged apps or scripts call your API as if they were the official app, bypassing client-side checks.
controls: Server-side enforcement of all rules
App attestation (Play Integrity / App Attest) for sensitive calls

interactor.title: Device identity of [name] can be cloned
interactor.desc: Devices share the same key or use guessable identifiers, so one extracted key lets attackers impersonate every device.
controls: Unique per-device keys or certificates, stored in secure hardware
Revocation per device

interactor.title: [name] receives more data than it needs
interactor.desc: Integrations send full records to partners when only a few fields are required, increasing exposure and breaching data-minimisation rules.
controls: Partner-specific APIs/views with only the needed fields
Data processing agreements and periodic review

interactor.title: Approvals by [name] are given outside the system
interactor.desc: Changes are approved in chat or email instead of in the tool, so there is no reliable record linking approval to change.
controls: Approvals recorded in the system of record
Link change records to approvers

interactor.title: Automated client [name] acts with a person's identity
interactor.desc: Scripts or integrations use a person's credentials, so automated actions look like human ones and cannot be separated.
controls: Dedicated service identities for automation
Mark automated actions in audit logs

interactor.title: Partner [name] disputes data it sent or received
interactor.desc: Without signed messages or delivery receipts, a partner can deny having sent or received an order or file.
controls: Message signing and acknowledgements for B2B exchanges
Keep exchanged messages with timestamps

interactor.title: Data shown to [name] exposed via screen sharing or onlookers
interactor.desc: Support and operations staff show customer data on shared screens, calls or in public places.
controls: Mask sensitive fields by default; reveal on demand with logging
Privacy screens and screen-sharing guidance

interactor.title: [name] copies data to personal email, cloud drives or AI tools
interactor.desc: Users move company or customer data into unsanctioned services where it is no longer protected or deletable.
controls: Data loss prevention for uploads and email
Provide approved tools, including approved AI assistants

interactor.title: Exports made by [name] stay on laptops and in inboxes
interactor.desc: CSV and report exports leave the system's access controls and retention.
controls: Limit and log exports; watermark reports
Expiry for shared export links

interactor.title: Device [name] connects to a server it does not authenticate
interactor.desc: Devices accept any server certificate or none, so a spoofed backend can send commands or firmware.
controls: Pin or validate the server certificate on the device
Mutual TLS between device and backend

interactor.title: Device [name] leaks data when sold, recycled or lost
interactor.desc: Credentials and data remain on devices that leave the organisation.
controls: Secure factory reset and remote wipe
Revoke device credentials at decommissioning

interactor.title: Compromised external identity provider [name] signs in as anyone
interactor.desc: Federation means you trust every login the provider asserts; if it is compromised, attackers can log in as any of your users.
controls: Limit which domains/tenants are trusted
Monitor federated logins; MFA enforced on your side for admins

interactor.title: Accounts from [name] are linked by email address alone
interactor.desc: Linking an external login to a local account just because the email matches lets someone who controls an unverified email address take over the account.
controls: Link accounts on the provider's stable subject ID
Require verified email and explicit linking by the user

interactor.title: Fake payment notifications pretending to come from [name]
interactor.desc: Forged callbacks or emails claim that a payment succeeded or a refund is due.
controls: Verify provider signatures; confirm status via the provider API
Never act on emailed payment confirmations alone

interactor.title: Payment provider [name] receives more customer data than needed
interactor.desc: Full customer profiles are sent where only an amount and reference are required.
controls: Send only fields the provider needs
Data processing agreement and review of shared fields

interactor.title: App [name] stores tokens or data insecurely on the device
interactor.desc: Tokens and personal data in plain files, shared preferences or logs are readable on rooted devices and in backups.
controls: Use the platform keystore/keychain for secrets
Exclude sensitive data from backups and logs

interactor.title: Logins via [name] cannot be matched to your own logs
interactor.desc: Your logs do not keep the provider's user and session identifiers, so a suspicious login there cannot be followed into your system.
controls: Log the IdP subject, session ID and authentication method
Keep IdP sign-in logs for the same period

interactor.title: Chargebacks via [name] cannot be contested
interactor.desc: Without evidence of authentication (3-D Secure), delivery and customer consent, disputed payments are lost.
controls: Keep authentication results, delivery proof and order history per payment
Use strong customer authentication where available

interactor.title: [name] signs in across a trust boundary with only a password
interactor.desc: Without a second factor, a phished, reused or guessed password is all an attacker needs to act as [name].
controls: Require MFA, preferably phishing-resistant (FIDO2/passkeys)
Block legacy protocols that cannot do MFA
Detect impossible travel and new-device sign-ins
interactor.example: Change Healthcare (2024): attackers used stolen credentials on a Citrix remote-access portal that had no MFA, then stole data and deployed ransomware; about 190 million people were affected.

interactor.title: Requests claiming to come from [name] are accepted without authentication
interactor.desc: A flow from [name] is not authenticated, so anyone who can reach the receiving component can send the same requests and be treated as [name].
controls: Authenticate every flow from external entities (OAuth2, signed requests, mTLS)
Bind sessions to the authenticated identity
Reject requests without valid credentials at the edge

interactor.title: Session or data of the previous user remains on [name]
interactor.desc: The next person at the shared terminal sees, or continues, the previous user's session, documents or form data.
controls: Automatic sign-out after inactivity and at session end
Wipe browser data and files between sessions
Clear visual cue when a session is still active

interactor.title: Stolen OAuth tokens of [name] used to pull your data
interactor.desc: Integrations hold long-lived OAuth or API tokens for your SaaS systems. When the integration vendor is breached, the attacker uses those tokens directly — no password or MFA involved.
controls: Inventory connected apps and their scopes; remove unused ones
Restrict tokens by IP and lifetime where possible
Monitor API exports by integrations; be ready to revoke all tokens quickly
interactor.example: Salesloft Drift (2025): attackers used stolen OAuth tokens of the Drift integration to export data from many companies' Salesforce instances and search it for further credentials.

interactor.title: Security provider [name] compromised and used as a way in
interactor.desc: Managed security providers and tools have privileged access to many customers at once, which makes them a valuable target.
controls: Limit provider access to what they need; time-bound privileged access
Monitor provider accounts like admins
Contractual security and incident-notification requirements

interactor.title: [name] receives all of your security telemetry
interactor.desc: Logs and telemetry sent to the provider include user names, internal hostnames and sometimes sensitive content.
controls: Agree on what is sent and how long it is kept
Filter sensitive fields before sending
Data-processing agreement

interactor.title: [name] is not authenticated at all
interactor.desc: Requests from this entity carry no proof of who sent them, so anyone can pretend to be it.
controls: Authenticate the entity (accounts, API keys, certificates)
Treat unauthenticated traffic as anonymous and limit what it can do

interactor.title: A fake fingerprint, photo or mask fools [name]
interactor.desc: Presentation attacks — printed photos, video replays, silicone fingers, deepfake video — are accepted as the real person.
controls: Liveness / presentation-attack detection tested to ISO/IEC 30107-3
Combine biometrics with a device or PIN for high-risk actions
Monitor and rate-limit failed attempts

interactor.title: Biometric data of [name] collected beyond its purpose
interactor.desc: Biometrics are special-category data; collecting them without a clear purpose, consent or alternative creates legal and trust problems.
controls: Data-protection impact assessment
Offer a non-biometric alternative
Delete templates when no longer needed

interactor.title: Attacker [name] logs in with leaked passwords (credential stuffing)
interactor.desc: Lists of usernames and passwords from other breaches are tried automatically against your login, and reused passwords work.
controls: MFA, or at least risk-based step-up for new devices
Check passwords against breach lists
Bot detection and rate limiting on login
interactor.example: 23andMe (2023): credential stuffing on about 14,000 accounts, combined with a relatives-sharing feature, exposed data of about 6.9 million people.

interactor.title: Attacker [name] harvests data through legitimate features
interactor.desc: Search, contact import, profile pages or exports are used at scale to collect data that each request alone was allowed to see.
controls: Rate limits and anomaly detection per account and feature
Return less data per request; avoid lookup-by-phone/email features
Monitor for enumeration patterns
interactor.example: Facebook (2021): data of about 533 million users, scraped through a contact-import feature in 2019, was published for free.

interactor.title: Activity by [name] cannot be linked across accounts and addresses
interactor.desc: An attacker rotates accounts, IP addresses and devices; without correlation every action looks unrelated.
controls: Correlate by device, behaviour and payment data
Keep enough history to link events
Fraud and abuse case management

interactor.title: Bot [name] creates fake accounts or takes over real ones at scale
interactor.desc: Automated clients sign up thousands of accounts for spam, promotions or fraud, or test stolen credentials (OWASP OAT-019, OAT-008).
controls: Bot management (device signals, behaviour) on sign-up and login
Verification steps proportional to risk
Rate limits per IP, device and account

interactor.title: Traffic from [name] cannot be told apart from real users
interactor.desc: Automated actions are logged exactly like human ones, so abuse cannot be separated or attributed.
controls: Log bot scores and client signals
Separate API keys for legitimate automation
Label known automation in logs

interactor.title: Company account on [name] taken over
interactor.desc: A hijacked company or executive account posts scams, fake announcements or malicious links to people who trust it.
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA on all company social and chat accounts
Managed access (no shared passwords); remove leavers
Monitoring of posts and login alerts
interactor.example: Twitter (2020): attackers phone-phished Twitter staff, used an internal admin tool to take over 130 high-profile accounts and posted a bitcoin scam.

interactor.title: Confidential data shared on [name]
interactor.desc: Staff paste customer data, credentials or plans into chats and channels that include external guests or are kept indefinitely.
controls: Guest and external-sharing policies
DLP and secret scanning on chat platforms
Retention limits

interactor.title: Attackers impersonate colleagues or IT support on [name]
interactor.desc: External users contact staff on chat platforms pretending to be the help desk or a manager, and talk them into installing remote-access tools or approving MFA prompts.
controls: Restrict who outside the organisation can message staff
Clear labels for external users
Train staff: IT will never ask for this over chat

interactor.title: Commitments made on [name] cannot be proven later
interactor.desc: Approvals, orders or advice given in chat are lost or deleted, so disputes cannot be resolved.
controls: Use proper systems for approvals
Retention and archiving where required by law
Export important conversations to records

interactor.title: [name] exchanges data over unencrypted channels
interactor.desc: The entity is marked as open: what it sends and receives can be read by anyone on the network path.
controls: Require TLS for every connection from this entity
Reject plaintext protocols at the edge

interactor.title: Actions with the shared key of [name] cannot be tied to a person
interactor.desc: Several people or systems use the same API key or certificate, so the log shows the key — not who used it.
controls: One credential per client or person
Log the key ID together with source and purpose
Rotate shared keys and phase them out

interactor.title: Session cookies from [name]'s browser stolen and replayed
interactor.desc: Malware, malicious extensions or XSS copy the session cookie, which works from another machine without password or MFA.
controls: Short session lifetimes; bind sessions to device where possible
HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies
Detect sessions used from new locations

interactor.title: Browser of [name] keeps sensitive data after use
interactor.desc: Autofill, browser history, cached pages and downloads keep sensitive data on shared or unmanaged computers.
controls: Cache-Control: no-store for sensitive pages
autocomplete="off" for sensitive fields
Session sign-out clears client-side storage

interactor.title: Traffic to [name] redirected by a DNS or BGP hijack
interactor.desc: Attackers announce your IP space or change DNS, sending users to an impostor that presents a convincing page or harvests connections.
controls: RPKI route-origin validation with your network providers
DNSSEC and registrar lock
HSTS and certificate monitoring (CT logs)
interactor.example: MyEtherWallet (2018): attackers hijacked Amazon Route 53 IP space via BGP, answered DNS for the site and redirected users to a phishing copy that stole cryptocurrency.

interactor.title: Network provider [name] can observe your traffic
interactor.desc: Internet providers, Wi-Fi hotspots and carriers see metadata and any unencrypted content.
controls: Encrypt everything in transit (TLS 1.2+), including internal links over provider networks
VPN or private links for sensitive site-to-site traffic

interactor.title: Emails pretending to come from [name] are delivered
interactor.desc: Without SPF, DKIM and an enforced DMARC policy, attackers send mail with the sender's domain in the From address.
controls: Publish SPF and DKIM; DMARC with p=reject
Flag external senders and lookalike domains
Verify payment changes out of band

interactor.title: Sensitive data emailed to the wrong recipient at [name]
interactor.desc: Autocomplete and reply-all send personal or confidential data to the wrong person — one of the most common reported data breaches.
controls: Warnings for external recipients; delayed send
Send links to access-controlled storage instead of attachments
DLP rules for sensitive content

interactor.title: Instructions received by email from [name] cannot be verified
interactor.desc: Changes of bank details, orders or approvals received by email are acted on without proof of who sent them (business email compromise).
controls: Confirm payment and contact changes via a known phone number
Require approvals in a system, not by email
Keep message headers for investigations

infrastructure.title: Default or shared credentials on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Devices, appliances and platforms shipped with default admin passwords — or one password shared across many devices — are taken over by automated scanning.
controls: Change defaults at install; unique credentials per device
Disable unused services (telnet, default admin UI)
infrastructure.example: Mirai (2016): malware logged into hundreds of thousands of IoT devices with default passwords and used them for record DDoS attacks.

infrastructure.title: Rogue device impersonates [name]
infrastructure.desc: A device spoofs this host's IP, MAC or hostname to receive traffic or join the network as a trusted machine.
controls: Network access control (802.1X), device certificates
Alert on duplicate addresses

infrastructure.title: Firmware or system configuration of [name] changed without detection
infrastructure.desc: Exposed management ports or missing secure boot let attackers modify firmware or configuration and persist.
controls: Secure boot; signed firmware updates
Configuration baselines with drift detection
Restrict management access

infrastructure.title: Logs from [name] are not collected centrally
infrastructure.desc: Host, network and cloud control-plane logs stay where an attacker can disable or delete them.
controls: Forward logs to a central SIEM in real time
Alert when logging is disabled or stops

infrastructure.title: Cloud instance credentials of [name] stolen via the metadata service
infrastructure.desc: Code running on the host — or an SSRF flaw — reads temporary cloud credentials from the instance metadata endpoint.
controls: Require IMDSv2 / metadata protection
Least-privilege instance roles
Block metadata access from containers that do not need it
infrastructure.example: Capital One (2019): credentials from the EC2 metadata service were used to read S3 data.

infrastructure.title: Secrets in plaintext on disks, images or snapshots of [name]
infrastructure.desc: Configuration files, scripts, VM images and snapshots contain passwords and keys readable by anyone with access to them.
controls: Secret manager; inject at runtime
Scan images and repositories for secrets
Encrypt disks and snapshots

infrastructure.title: Lost or stolen [name] exposes its data
infrastructure.desc: Laptops, devices and disks that leave the building — lost, stolen or decommissioned — still contain readable data.
controls: Full-disk encryption
Remote wipe; secure decommissioning

infrastructure.title: Single instance of [name] with no redundancy
infrastructure.desc: One host, zone or network path failing — or being attacked — takes the whole service down.
controls: Redundancy across zones
Health checks and automatic failover
Tested recovery procedures

infrastructure.title: Other workloads exhaust shared resources of [name]
infrastructure.desc: Neighbouring workloads on the same host, cluster or account consume CPU, memory or quotas.
controls: Resource limits and reservations
Separate accounts or clusters for critical workloads

infrastructure.title: Management interface of [name] reachable from an untrusted network
infrastructure.desc: SSH, RDP, Kubernetes API, hypervisor or admin consoles are reachable across a trust boundary and are attacked with stolen credentials and exploits.
controls: Management only via VPN/bastion/zero-trust access
MFA on all administrative access
Allow-list source addresses

infrastructure.title: Unpatched OS or services on [name] allow remote takeover
infrastructure.desc: Known vulnerabilities in the operating system or exposed services are exploited to run code with high privileges.
controls: Patch management with SLAs
Minimise exposed services
Vulnerability scanning

infrastructure.title: Container escape from [name] to the host
infrastructure.desc: Privileged containers, mounted host paths or kernel flaws let code inside a container take over the host and its other containers.
controls: No privileged containers or host mounts
Run as non-root; seccomp/AppArmor
Patch the host kernel and runtime

infrastructure.title: Flat network lets attackers move from [name] to other systems
infrastructure.desc: Once one machine is compromised, nothing stops connections to databases, admin systems and other hosts.
controls: Network segmentation and default-deny between zones
Monitor east-west traffic
infrastructure.example: Target (2013): attackers moved from a vendor portal to point-of-sale systems inside the network.

infrastructure.title: Exploitable VPN or edge appliance [name]
infrastructure.desc: Internet-facing VPNs, gateways and firewalls are prime targets; pre-authentication vulnerabilities give attackers a foothold inside the network.
controls: Patch within days for edge devices; subscribe to vendor advisories
Restrict management interfaces; monitor for integrity changes
Terminate sessions after patching
infrastructure.example: Ivanti Connect Secure (2024, CVE-2023-46805 + CVE-2024-21887) was mass-exploited for unauthenticated command execution. Citrix Bleed (2023, CVE-2023-4966) leaked session tokens that bypassed MFA.

infrastructure.title: DNS for [name] hijacked through the registrar or DNS provider account
infrastructure.desc: Taking over the DNS or registrar account lets attackers point your domains at their servers and obtain valid certificates.
controls: MFA and restricted access on registrar/DNS accounts; registry lock
Monitor DNS record changes and certificate issuance (CT logs)

infrastructure.title: Dangling DNS records allow subdomain takeover
infrastructure.desc: Records still point at deleted cloud resources (apps, buckets, CDN endpoints), which attackers can claim to serve content on your subdomain.
controls: Remove DNS records when resources are deleted
Scan for dangling CNAMEs regularly

infrastructure.title: Web cache deception or poisoning on [name]
infrastructure.desc: The CDN caches personalised pages under static-looking URLs, or caches responses influenced by unkeyed headers, serving them to other users.
controls: Cache only explicitly cacheable paths; respect Cache-Control
Normalise and key on all inputs that change the response

infrastructure.title: Overly permissive Kubernetes RBAC on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Service accounts or users have cluster-admin, wildcard or secrets-read permissions, so one compromised pod controls the cluster.
controls: Least-privilege roles per namespace; no wildcard verbs
Disable automounting service account tokens where not needed

infrastructure.title: Kubernetes secrets on [name] readable by too many
infrastructure.desc: Secrets are only base64-encoded, not encrypted at rest, and readable by broad roles or anyone with node access.
controls: Encryption at rest for secrets (KMS provider)
External secret store; restrict get/list on secrets

infrastructure.title: Long-lived cloud access keys for [name] leak
infrastructure.desc: Static access keys in laptops, CI systems or repositories are copied and used from anywhere.
controls: Short-lived role-based credentials (SSO, workload identity)
Key age alerts and automatic rotation
Secret scanning

infrastructure.title: Disk snapshots or images of [name] shared publicly
infrastructure.desc: Snapshots, AMIs or images are made public or shared with other accounts, exposing their full disk contents.
controls: Block public sharing at account level
Encrypt snapshots with customer-managed keys

infrastructure.title: Directory service [name] compromised (Kerberoasting, weak service accounts)
infrastructure.desc: Service accounts with weak passwords and broad rights can be cracked offline from Kerberos tickets, leading to domain-wide control.
controls: Long random passwords or managed service accounts
Tiered administration; monitor for ticket requests from unusual hosts

infrastructure.title: Unpatched mail server [name] exploited
infrastructure.desc: Internet-facing mail servers are frequently exploited for remote code execution and mailbox access.
controls: Patch quickly or move to a managed mail service
Restrict admin and web endpoints
infrastructure.example: Microsoft Exchange ProxyLogon (2021, CVE-2021-26855): mass exploitation of on-premises Exchange servers.

infrastructure.title: Unsigned firmware updates on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Devices accept firmware updates that are not signed or are downloaded over plain HTTP, so attackers can install their own firmware.
controls: Signed firmware verified on the device
Updates over TLS; anti-rollback

infrastructure.title: Debug ports on [name] give a root shell
infrastructure.desc: UART, JTAG or test interfaces left enabled let anyone with physical access read firmware and secrets or take control.
controls: Disable or lock debug interfaces in production
Store keys in secure elements

infrastructure.title: [name] can be abused to amplify DDoS attacks
infrastructure.desc: Open UDP services (DNS resolvers, NTP, memcached) answer spoofed requests with much larger responses aimed at a victim.
controls: Do not expose UDP services to the internet; disable recursion for public DNS
Source address validation (BCP 38)
infrastructure.example: GitHub (2018): a 1.35 Tbps attack used publicly exposed memcached servers as amplifiers.

infrastructure.title: Manual changes to [name] bypass infrastructure-as-code
infrastructure.desc: Hand-made changes drift from the reviewed configuration and silently undo security settings.
controls: Infrastructure as code with review; restrict console write access
Drift detection and alerts

infrastructure.title: Firewall or security group rules on [name] opened too widely
infrastructure.desc: "Temporary" allow-any rules or 0.0.0.0/0 exposures remain in place long after they were needed.
controls: Rule review and expiry dates; least-open rules
Automated checks for wide-open rules

infrastructure.title: No admission control on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Anyone who can deploy can run privileged or unverified workloads, because no central policy checks them.
controls: Admission policies (e.g. Kyverno/OPA Gatekeeper) for images, privileges and labels
Signed images only

infrastructure.title: Tampered VM or container images deployed to [name]
infrastructure.desc: Images pulled from public registries or shared accounts without signature checks may contain backdoors.
controls: Private registry; verify image signatures
Approved base images only

infrastructure.title: Cloud control-plane activity for [name] not logged
infrastructure.desc: API activity logs (e.g. CloudTrail / Activity Log) are disabled, short-lived or writable by the admins they record.
controls: Organisation-wide control-plane logging to a separate account
Alert when logging is changed

infrastructure.title: Shared admin accounts on [name]
infrastructure.desc: The team shares one admin or root login, so actions cannot be tied to a person.
controls: Individual admin accounts; vault shared break-glass credentials
Session recording for privileged access

infrastructure.title: No network flow logs for [name]
infrastructure.desc: Without flow logs, connections to and from the system cannot be reconstructed after an incident.
controls: Enable VPC/firewall flow logs for critical segments
Retain and centralise them

infrastructure.title: Expired certificate or domain takes [name] offline
infrastructure.desc: TLS certificates or domain registrations that are not renewed in time cause sudden outages.
controls: Automated certificate renewal (ACME)
Expiry monitoring for certificates and domains
infrastructure.example: Microsoft Teams (February 2020): an expired authentication certificate caused a multi-hour outage.

infrastructure.title: Cloud quotas or account suspension take [name] offline
infrastructure.desc: Hitting service quotas, unpaid bills or an abuse-triggered suspension stops everything in the account.
controls: Quota monitoring and increases ahead of growth
Billing alerts; separate accounts for critical workloads

infrastructure.title: ARP or DHCP spoofing on the network of [name]
infrastructure.desc: An attacker on the local network answers ARP or DHCP requests and routes traffic through their machine.
controls: Dynamic ARP inspection and DHCP snooping on switches
Encrypt traffic even on internal networks

infrastructure.title: Rogue Wi-Fi access point imitates [name]
infrastructure.desc: An "evil twin" network with the same name captures logins and traffic from devices that connect automatically.
controls: WPA3-Enterprise with certificate validation
Wireless intrusion detection

infrastructure.title: VPN [name] accepts passwords without MFA
infrastructure.desc: One phished or reused password gives full network access.
controls: MFA for every VPN login; remove legacy accounts
Device certificates or posture checks

infrastructure.title: VPN users of [name] can reach the whole network
infrastructure.desc: After connecting, users and compromised laptops reach every internal system, not just what they need.
controls: Per-group access policies / zero-trust network access
Segment sensitive systems behind additional controls

infrastructure.title: Too many domain admin accounts on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Privileged directory accounts are numerous and used for everyday work, so any compromised workstation can expose them.
controls: Minimise domain admins; separate admin accounts
Privileged access workstations and tiering

infrastructure.title: Password hashes extracted from [name] (DCSync / NTDS.dit)
infrastructure.desc: Attackers with replication rights or disk access copy all password hashes and reuse them.
controls: Restrict replication rights; monitor DCSync requests
Protect domain controller backups

infrastructure.title: Mail server [name] is an open relay
infrastructure.desc: The server accepts mail for any recipient from anyone, so it is used for spam and phishing in your name.
controls: Relay only for authenticated users and own domains
Regular open-relay checks

infrastructure.title: Mailboxes on [name] accessible through legacy protocols without MFA
infrastructure.desc: IMAP, POP or basic-auth protocols bypass MFA and are used for password spraying and mailbox theft.
controls: Disable legacy/basic authentication
Conditional access for mail clients

infrastructure.title: Same local admin password on [name] and other machines
infrastructure.desc: A shared local administrator password lets an attacker who compromises one machine log into all others (pass-the-hash).
controls: Unique, rotated local admin passwords (LAPS)
Restrict local admin logons over the network

infrastructure.title: No endpoint detection or integrity monitoring on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Malware and persistence mechanisms (new services, scheduled tasks) go unnoticed.
controls: Endpoint detection and response
File integrity monitoring on critical servers

infrastructure.title: Origin behind [name] reachable directly, bypassing CDN and WAF
infrastructure.desc: If the origin server accepts traffic from anywhere, attackers skip the WAF, rate limits and DDoS protection.
controls: Allow only CDN IP ranges or authenticated origin pulls
Keep the origin address private

infrastructure.title: Configuration changes on [name] are not tracked
infrastructure.desc: Network device or appliance configs are changed without versioning, so nobody can tell who opened a rule or when.
controls: Configuration backups with diffs and change tickets
Syslog of configuration commands to a central store

infrastructure.title: Traffic to and from [name] crosses a boundary without being inspected or restricted
infrastructure.desc: [name] has connections across a trust boundary but no explicit allow-list of what may pass, so any service on it is reachable and exfiltration is not noticed.
controls: Default-deny firewall or security-group rules with an owner per rule
Egress filtering to known destinations
Flow logs reviewed for unexpected destinations

infrastructure.title: Configuration file [name] exposes secrets
infrastructure.desc: .env, YAML or JSON configuration holds database passwords, cloud keys or API tokens and ends up readable — served by the web server, committed to git, baked into an image or attached to a ticket.
controls: Keep secrets in a secrets manager and reference them, not in config files
Block dotfiles and config paths at the web server
Secret scanning in repositories and images
Rotate any secret that was ever in a config file
infrastructure.example: Exposed .env files (2024): an extortion campaign reported by Palo Alto Unit 42 scanned about 230 million targets for public .env files, harvested over 1,100 AWS keys and other tokens, and ransomed data from cloud storage.

infrastructure.title: Changing [name] changes security behaviour
infrastructure.desc: Whoever can edit the configuration can point the application at another endpoint, switch off authentication or TLS checks, or enable debug features — no code change needed.
controls: Read-only configuration at runtime; changes only through review and deployment
Integrity monitoring or signed configuration
Separate high-risk settings (auth, TLS, endpoints) and alert on their change

infrastructure.title: Changes to [name] are not versioned or reviewed
infrastructure.desc: Configuration is edited in place, so when something breaks or a security setting is weakened nobody can see who changed what, or roll back.
controls: Configuration as code in version control with mandatory review
Change records linked to deployments
Diff-based alerts for production configuration

infrastructure.title: A bad configuration change in [name] takes services down
infrastructure.desc: A typo, wrong value or untested change is pushed everywhere at once and breaks every instance that reads it.
controls: Validate configuration (schema, test environment) before release
Staged roll-out with automatic rollback
Keep the last known-good configuration available

infrastructure.title: Insecure defaults left in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Debug mode, sample accounts, default passwords or open admin consoles from the default configuration are still enabled in production.
controls: Hardened baseline configuration (e.g. CIS Benchmarks)
Configuration scanning in the pipeline
Remove samples and default accounts on install

infrastructure.title: Private keys controlling [name] stolen
infrastructure.desc: Whoever holds the signing keys (or enough of the validator or multisig keys) can move funds or write to the ledger, and transactions cannot be reversed.
controls: Keys in HSMs or MPC wallets, never on ordinary servers
Threshold signing with independent operators; remove stale delegated signers
Withdrawal limits and time delays for large transfers
infrastructure.example: Ronin Network (2022): attackers obtained five of the nine validator keys — including one delegated permission that was never revoked — and withdrew about $625 million.

infrastructure.title: Smart contract flaw lets attackers drain or alter [name]
infrastructure.desc: Logic or access-control bugs (reentrancy, unchecked callers, price-oracle manipulation) in deployed contracts are exploited, and the code cannot simply be patched.
controls: Independent audits and formal verification of contracts
Pause / circuit-breaker functions with multisig control
Bug bounty and on-chain monitoring of unusual calls
infrastructure.example: Poly Network (2021): a flaw in a cross-chain contract call let an attacker replace the trusted keeper and take about $610 million (most was later returned).

infrastructure.title: Personal data written to [name] can never be erased
infrastructure.desc: Ledgers are append-only and replicated to every node, so personal data written there cannot be corrected or deleted when the law requires it.
controls: Keep personal data off-chain; store only hashes or references
Salted hashes so values cannot be guessed
Data-protection review before anything personal is written

infrastructure.title: Abnormal transfers from [name] go unnoticed
infrastructure.desc: Nobody watches the ledger for unusual withdrawals, so a theft is discovered only when users complain — days later.
controls: Real-time monitoring and alerts on large or unusual transfers
Reconcile on-chain balances with internal records
Incident playbook for freezing bridges or contracts

infrastructure.title: Data copied to [name] leaves the building unencrypted
infrastructure.desc: USB sticks, SD cards and external drives are small, often unencrypted and easily lost or taken out of the building.
controls: Enforce encryption on removable media (e.g. BitLocker To Go)
Allow only approved devices; block mass storage where not needed
DLP rules for copying sensitive data

infrastructure.title: Malware spreads through [name]
infrastructure.desc: Infected media runs malware when it is plugged in or a file on it is opened, and can bridge networks that are otherwise isolated.
controls: Disable autorun; scan media on insertion
Block execution from removable drives
Dedicated, scanned transfer stations for isolated networks
infrastructure.example: Raspberry Robin (2022): a worm spread through infected USB drives with a malicious shortcut file; Microsoft found it on devices in almost 1,000 organisations and linked it to later ransomware.

infrastructure.title: Copies to and from [name] are not recorded
infrastructure.desc: Nobody can tell which files were copied to or from the device, or by whom, when data turns up where it should not.
controls: Device control with audit logs of file copies
Tie device use to named users
Keep the logs long enough to investigate

infrastructure.title: Data on [name] readable after loss, decommissioning or snapshotting
infrastructure.desc: A disk that leaves its machine — returned, sold, recycled, or copied as a snapshot — still holds readable data if it was not encrypted or wiped.
controls: Full-disk encryption with keys in a TPM or KMS
Certified wiping (NIST SP 800-88) or destruction before disposal
Encrypted snapshots with restricted sharing

infrastructure.title: Disk failure or a wiper destroys [name]
infrastructure.desc: A failing drive, a corrupted file system or wiper malware deletes the data, and the newest usable copy is old or missing.
controls: Redundancy (RAID, replication) plus independent backups
Disk health monitoring
Restore tests

infrastructure.title: Offline tampering with [name] by booting another system
infrastructure.desc: With physical access, an attacker boots another operating system or moves the disk to another machine and changes files, adds accounts or plants malware.
controls: Full-disk encryption with pre-boot authentication
Secure Boot and firmware passwords
Physical security for the machine

infrastructure.title: Malicious update of a third-party package used by [name]
infrastructure.desc: A maintainer account is taken over, a maintainer turns malicious, or a lookalike package is published — and the next build of [name] pulls in the backdoor.
controls: Pin versions and verify checksums (lock files)
Delay adoption of brand-new versions; review diffs of critical dependencies
Private mirror with malware scanning
Track dependencies with an SBOM
infrastructure.example: xz utils (2024, CVE-2024-3094): a contributor who had gained maintainer trust over two years hid a backdoor targeting SSH servers in release tarballs; it was caught shortly before reaching stable Linux distributions.

infrastructure.title: Plugin or extension runs with the full rights of [name]
infrastructure.desc: Plugins are loaded into the same process without isolation, so a vulnerable or malicious plugin can do anything the host application can.
controls: Allow only reviewed plugins from trusted sources
Isolate plugins (separate process, sandbox, restricted APIs)
Keep plugins updated and remove unused ones

infrastructure.title: No provenance for artifacts in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Nobody can prove which source commit and which build produced an artifact, so a tampered or rebuilt artifact cannot be detected after the fact.
controls: Build provenance attestations (SLSA)
Record source commit, builder and checksums per artifact
Keep build logs

infrastructure.title: Private packages or images in [name] downloadable by anyone
infrastructure.desc: The registry or bucket allows anonymous pulls, exposing source code, internal endpoints and secrets baked into images.
controls: Require authentication to pull private packages
Scan images and packages for secrets before publishing
Regular review of public repositories

infrastructure.title: Scheduled job [name] runs attacker-controlled code with high rights
infrastructure.desc: The job runs as root or a service admin, and its script, schedule or working directory can be changed by others — an easy path to persistence and privilege escalation.
controls: Run jobs with a dedicated low-privilege account
Scripts and schedules writable only by administrators
Monitor changes to cron, systemd timers and scheduled tasks

infrastructure.title: Runs and failures of [name] are not recorded
infrastructure.desc: There is no record of when the job ran, with which input and what it changed, and failures are silent.
controls: Log start, end, inputs and result of every run
Heartbeat monitoring that alerts when a run is missed or fails
Keep run history

infrastructure.title: Overlapping or runaway runs of [name] exhaust resources
infrastructure.desc: A run takes longer than its interval, so runs pile up; or a bad input makes one run loop for hours and block everything else.
controls: Locking so only one run is active
Timeouts and resource limits per run
Back-pressure on input volume

infrastructure.title: Input files or records for [name] can be planted
infrastructure.desc: Batch jobs pick up whatever is in a shared folder, bucket or staging table, so anyone who can write there controls what is processed.
controls: Restrict who can write to the input location
Validate and authenticate input (checksums, signatures, schema)
Quarantine and reject unexpected files

infrastructure.title: Untrusted model files run code when [name] loads them
infrastructure.desc: Common model formats (Python pickle in PyTorch .pt/.bin, some Keras files) can execute code on load. Downloading a model from a public hub is running someone else's program.
controls: Prefer safe formats (safetensors, ONNX) and refuse pickle from untrusted sources
Scan models before use; pin by hash
Load models in a sandbox without credentials or network
infrastructure.example: Hugging Face (2024): JFrog found about 100 models on the hub with malicious payloads, including ones that opened a reverse shell as soon as the PyTorch file was loaded.

infrastructure.title: Cluster or notebook API of [name] runs jobs for anyone who can reach it
infrastructure.desc: Distributed compute frameworks and notebooks (Ray, Jupyter, MLflow) often ship without authentication; anyone on the network can submit code.
controls: Never expose these services to the internet; put them behind authenticated access
Enable built-in authentication where it exists
Network policies limiting who can reach the dashboard and job APIs
infrastructure.example: ShadowRay (2024): attackers used the unauthenticated Ray Jobs API (CVE-2023-48022, disputed by the vendor) to take over hundreds of AI clusters, steal credentials and run cryptominers.

infrastructure.title: GPU memory of [name] leaks data between users or jobs
infrastructure.desc: Memory on shared GPUs is not always cleared between processes, so one tenant can read another tenant's model responses or data.
controls: Dedicated GPUs or strong isolation (MIG, VMs) for sensitive workloads
Apply driver and firmware updates
Do not mix trusted and untrusted jobs on one GPU
infrastructure.example: LeftoverLocals (2024, CVE-2023-4969): Trail of Bits showed that leftover GPU local memory on several vendors' GPUs let one process reconstruct another user's LLM responses.

infrastructure.title: Training or fine-tuning data for [name] poisoned
infrastructure.desc: Manipulated training data plants a backdoor or bias in the model, which then behaves normally except on the attacker's trigger.
controls: Control and record where training data comes from
Validate and de-duplicate datasets; look for outliers
Evaluate models against known triggers before release

infrastructure.title: Cryptominers or runaway jobs consume [name]
infrastructure.desc: Expensive GPU capacity is hijacked for mining or burned by unbounded jobs, causing outages for real work and large bills.
controls: Quotas and budgets with alerts
Monitor GPU utilisation per job and owner
Restrict who can submit jobs

infrastructure.title: Model weights or datasets on [name] copied out
infrastructure.desc: Weights, checkpoints and training sets are valuable intellectual property and often contain personal data, but are stored in buckets and shared volumes with broad access.
controls: Access control and encryption for model and dataset storage
Egress controls and download monitoring
Treat training data under the same rules as production data

infrastructure.title: Users break out of kiosk [name] to the operating system
infrastructure.desc: Print dialogs, help links, file pickers or keyboard shortcuts let a user leave the kiosk application and reach the desktop, a shell or the network.
controls: Use the platform's assigned-access / kiosk mode
Disable shortcuts, dialogs and external links
Least-privilege local account; no network access beyond what is needed

infrastructure.title: Session or data of the previous user remains on [name]
infrastructure.desc: The next person at the shared terminal sees, or continues, the previous user's session, documents or form data.
controls: Automatic sign-out after inactivity and at session end
Wipe browser data and files between sessions
Clear visual cue when a session is still active

infrastructure.title: Skimmers, USB devices or overlays added to [name]
infrastructure.desc: Unattended terminals are physically tampered with: card skimmers, keyloggers, rogue USB devices or fake screens.
controls: Tamper-evident enclosures and seals; regular inspection
Disable unused ports
Alert on device changes and reboots

infrastructure.title: Infostealer on [name] steals saved passwords and session cookies
infrastructure.desc: Malware from cracked software, fake updates or malicious ads copies browser passwords and session cookies, which are sold and used to log in to company systems — often from a personal or unmanaged device.
controls: Managed devices with EDR for access to company systems
Phishing-resistant MFA and short session lifetimes; bind sessions to the device
Do not allow saving work passwords in browsers; use a password manager

infrastructure.title: Users are local administrators on [name]
infrastructure.desc: With local admin rights, any malware the user runs can disable protection, install drivers and dump credentials.
controls: Remove standing local admin rights; use just-in-time elevation
Application allow-listing for privileged tools
Unique local admin passwords (e.g. Windows LAPS)

infrastructure.title: Malicious macros, extensions or downloads run on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Office macros, browser extensions and downloaded tools run with the user's rights and change files, settings or browser sessions.
controls: Block macros from the internet; allow only signed macros
Allow-list browser extensions
Attack-surface-reduction rules and EDR

infrastructure.title: Injection flaws in the code of [name]
infrastructure.desc: User input is concatenated into SQL, shell commands, templates or file paths.
controls: Parameterised queries and safe APIs
Static analysis (SAST) in the pipeline
Allow-list input validation

infrastructure.title: Secrets committed in the code of [name]
infrastructure.desc: Keys and passwords committed to the repository stay in its history forever and spread to every clone, fork and CI log.
controls: Secret scanning with push protection
Rotate exposed secrets immediately; history rewrites are not enough
Load secrets from a secrets manager at runtime
infrastructure.example: Uber (2016): attackers found cloud credentials in a private GitHub repository and used them to download data of about 57 million riders and drivers.

infrastructure.title: Vulnerable dependencies in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Libraries with known remote-code-execution flaws stay in the code because nobody tracks or updates them.
controls: Software composition analysis with alerts
Automated dependency updates
SBOM for every release

infrastructure.title: Code changes to [name] merged without review
infrastructure.desc: One person can change production code alone, so a malicious or mistaken change cannot be attributed to a deliberate decision.
controls: Protected branches with required review
Signed commits
Separate approver for releases

infrastructure.title: Command injection through arguments or variables in [name]
infrastructure.desc: File names, user input or environment values are expanded unquoted in shell or PowerShell commands, so a crafted value runs extra commands.
controls: Quote all variables; avoid eval and string-built commands
Use a real programming language with argument arrays for anything non-trivial
Lint scripts (ShellCheck, PSScriptAnalyzer)

infrastructure.title: Script [name] runs with high rights from a location others can write
infrastructure.desc: An administrator or scheduler runs the script, but the script file, the folder or a tool it calls can be modified by ordinary users.
controls: Store privileged scripts in admin-only locations
Use absolute paths; do not trust PATH or the working directory
Sign scripts and enforce signature checks

infrastructure.title: [name] downloads and runs code without checking it
infrastructure.desc: Patterns like curl | bash or Invoke-Expression on a downloaded string run whatever the server returns at that moment.
controls: Download, verify checksum or signature, then run
Pin versions of downloaded tools
Host internal copies of third-party scripts

infrastructure.title: Who ran [name] and with which arguments is not logged
infrastructure.desc: Scripts run by people or tools leave no record, so misuse cannot be investigated.
controls: Enable script block / command logging (e.g. PowerShell logging)
Run privileged scripts through a tool that records the operator
Send logs to central storage

infrastructure.title: Test environment [name] has weaker sign-in but reaches production
infrastructure.desc: Test and legacy environments skip MFA and monitoring, yet hold accounts, apps or credentials with rights in production.
controls: Same identity controls (MFA, conditional access) for non-production
No production permissions from test tenants, apps or accounts
Inventory and decommission legacy test environments
infrastructure.example: Microsoft (2024): Midnight Blizzard password-sprayed a legacy non-production test tenant account without MFA, then abused a test OAuth app to read corporate mailboxes.

infrastructure.title: Real customer data copied into [name]
infrastructure.desc: Production data is copied to test so that tests are realistic, but test has broader access, weaker logging and more people.
controls: Synthetic or masked data for test
If real data is unavoidable, the same controls as production
Automatic expiry of test copies

infrastructure.title: Debug features left enabled in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Debug endpoints, verbose errors, heap-dump or actuator endpoints and test backdoors expose internals and secrets.
controls: Disable debug features in builds that leave the developer machine
Block management endpoints at the gateway
Scan for debug endpoints before release

infrastructure.title: Shared credentials or network paths connect [name] to production
infrastructure.desc: The same service accounts, keys or open network routes are used in test and production, so compromising the weaker environment gives the stronger one.
controls: Separate accounts, keys and cloud subscriptions per environment
No network routes from test to production
Different secrets per environment

infrastructure.title: Stolen OAuth tokens of [name] used to pull your data
infrastructure.desc: Integrations hold long-lived OAuth or API tokens for your SaaS systems. When the integration vendor is breached, the attacker uses those tokens directly — no password or MFA involved.
controls: Inventory connected apps and their scopes; remove unused ones
Restrict tokens by IP and lifetime where possible
Monitor API exports by integrations; be ready to revoke all tokens quickly
infrastructure.example: Salesloft Drift (2025): attackers used stolen OAuth tokens of the Drift integration to export data from many companies' Salesforce instances and search it for further credentials.

infrastructure.title: Integration [name] has broader scopes than it uses
infrastructure.desc: Connectors are granted admin or full-access scopes during set-up "to make it work", so a flaw in the connector reaches everything.
controls: Grant the narrowest scopes; review them at each change
Dedicated integration accounts per connector
Periodic access review of non-human identities

infrastructure.title: Data passed by [name] between systems is not validated
infrastructure.desc: The connector maps fields from one system to another and trusts both sides, carrying injected or malformed data into systems that assume it was checked.
controls: Validate against the target system's schema and rules
Reject and quarantine unexpected values
Encode data for the target context

infrastructure.title: Actions by [name] appear as a generic service account
infrastructure.desc: Everything the integration does is logged as one technical user, so you cannot tell which person or triggering event caused a change.
controls: Pass and log the originating user or event ID
One service identity per integration
Keep integration run logs

infrastructure.title: [name] fails silently and data stops syncing
infrastructure.desc: Expired credentials, API changes or rate limits stop the integration, and nobody notices until records are missing.
controls: Health checks and alerts on sync lag
Dead-letter queues and retry with back-off
Credential expiry monitoring

infrastructure.title: Monitoring tool [name] exposes data-source credentials and internals
infrastructure.desc: Dashboards hold credentials for databases and cloud accounts, and show architecture details; an exposed or vulnerable instance gives all of that away.
controls: Never expose monitoring tools to the internet; require SSO
Patch promptly — these tools are actively targeted
Read-only, least-privilege data-source credentials
infrastructure.example: Grafana (CVE-2021-43798): an unauthenticated path traversal let attackers read files such as grafana.ini and the Grafana database from self-hosted servers; CISA lists it as exploited.

infrastructure.title: Attackers silence alerts or change thresholds in [name]
infrastructure.desc: An attacker with access to the monitoring system mutes alerts, deletes rules or raises thresholds before acting.
controls: Alert on changes to alert rules and notification channels
Separate admin rights for monitoring configuration
Monitor the monitoring (dead-man's switch)

infrastructure.title: Monitoring agents of [name] run as root and accept remote commands
infrastructure.desc: Agents installed on every host run with full rights and can execute actions pushed from the central server — a compromise of the server is a compromise of every host.
controls: Disable remote command features you do not use
Restrict and audit who can push actions
Run agents with minimal rights where supported

infrastructure.title: Alert floods or an outage of [name] hide real incidents
infrastructure.desc: Too many noisy alerts, or the monitoring system being down, mean a real attack or outage is not seen in time.
controls: Tune alerts; route by severity
Redundant monitoring for critical signals
External uptime checks

infrastructure.title: Data warehouse [name] reachable with stolen passwords and no MFA
infrastructure.desc: Analytics platforms hold copies of everything, are reachable from the internet, and are often accessed with long-lived passwords without MFA or network restrictions.
controls: Enforce MFA or key-pair / SSO authentication for every user
Network policies limiting access to known locations
Rotate and expire credentials; alert on bulk exports
infrastructure.example: Snowflake customers (2024): attackers used credentials stolen by infostealer malware to log in to over 100 customer accounts that had no MFA, and stole large datasets for extortion.

infrastructure.title: Analysts can query personal data in [name] they do not need
infrastructure.desc: Raw personal data is loaded into the warehouse and everyone with access can query it, far beyond the original purpose.
controls: Pseudonymise or mask personal data on load
Row- and column-level security
Purpose-based access reviews

infrastructure.title: Runaway queries in [name] exhaust capacity or budget
infrastructure.desc: A single heavy query or a loop in a dashboard uses all credits or slots and blocks other users.
controls: Resource monitors, quotas and budgets
Query timeouts
Separate compute for heavy workloads

infrastructure.title: Security product [name] itself is exploited
infrastructure.desc: Security tools run with the highest privileges and sit at network edges, so a flaw in them gives an attacker exactly the position they want.
controls: Patch security products as fast as anything internet-facing
Restrict their management interfaces
Include them in vulnerability scanning and monitoring

infrastructure.title: Attackers disable or reconfigure [name]
infrastructure.desc: Attackers who gain admin rights turn off protection, add exclusions or change policies before deploying malware.
controls: Tamper protection; changes only with separate admin approval
Alert when protection is disabled or exclusions are added
Separate admin accounts for security tools

infrastructure.title: A faulty update of [name] takes down the systems it protects
infrastructure.desc: Security software updates itself automatically and runs deep in the system; one bad update can crash every machine at once.
controls: Staged roll-out of agent and content updates where the vendor allows
Tested recovery procedures (boot media, recovery keys available)
Ask vendors how updates are tested and staged
infrastructure.example: CrowdStrike (July 2024): a faulty content update for the Falcon sensor crashed about 8.5 million Windows machines, halting airlines, hospitals and banks.

infrastructure.title: Alerts from [name] are not reviewed or kept
infrastructure.desc: The control detects suspicious activity, but nobody looks at the alerts and they expire before an incident is investigated.
controls: Route alerts to a monitored queue with an owner
Retain alerts and events long enough to investigate
Measure time to triage

infrastructure.title: [name] is readable without authentication or encryption
infrastructure.desc: The component is marked as open: anyone who can reach it, or listen to the network, can read its data.
controls: Require authentication for every access
Encrypt in transit and at rest
Restrict network access to known clients

infrastructure.title: Anyone can change data in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Without authentication and integrity protection, any reachable client can write or alter data.
controls: Authenticated, authorised writes only
Integrity checks (signatures, checksums) on stored data
Audit writes

infrastructure.title: Biometric data in [name] leaks — and cannot be changed
infrastructure.desc: Fingerprints and face templates are permanent: once leaked, they cannot be reset like a password. Many systems also store them unencrypted next to names and access rights.
controls: Store templates encrypted and separately from identities; prefer on-device matching
Never store raw images when templates suffice
Strict access control and data-protection impact assessment
infrastructure.example: Suprema BioStar 2 (2019): researchers found an unprotected database with over a million fingerprint records, face images and unencrypted passwords used by building access systems.

infrastructure.title: A fake fingerprint, photo or mask fools [name]
infrastructure.desc: Presentation attacks — printed photos, video replays, silicone fingers, deepfake video — are accepted as the real person.
controls: Liveness / presentation-attack detection tested to ISO/IEC 30107-3
Combine biometrics with a device or PIN for high-risk actions
Monitor and rate-limit failed attempts

infrastructure.title: Biometric reader [name] fails with no fallback
infrastructure.desc: When the reader or matching service is down, people are locked out — or staff prop doors open.
controls: Defined fallback (card + PIN) with the same assurance
Monitor reader health
Spare devices for critical doors

infrastructure.title: Ransomware on [name] encrypts everything it can reach
infrastructure.desc: Malicious code running on this component encrypts its data and every share and backup reachable with its credentials.
controls: Least-privilege access to shares and backups
Immutable backups
EDR with ransomware protection; segment the network

infrastructure.title: Attacker-controlled [name] exfiltrates data
infrastructure.desc: A compromised or malicious component sends data out through allowed channels (HTTPS, DNS, cloud storage).
controls: Egress filtering and proxying
DLP and anomaly detection on outbound volumes
Alert on new destinations

infrastructure.title: Bot [name] creates fake accounts or takes over real ones at scale
infrastructure.desc: Automated clients sign up thousands of accounts for spam, promotions or fraud, or test stolen credentials (OWASP OAT-019, OAT-008).
controls: Bot management (device signals, behaviour) on sign-up and login
Verification steps proportional to risk
Rate limits per IP, device and account

infrastructure.title: Bot [name] scrapes content and prices
infrastructure.desc: Automated scraping copies content, prices or personal data in bulk (OWASP OAT-011).
controls: Rate limiting and bot detection
Serve less data per request; require sign-in for valuable data
Monitor for scraping patterns

infrastructure.title: Bot traffic from [name] exhausts capacity or stock
infrastructure.desc: Scalper and inventory-hoarding bots buy or reserve limited items and overload checkout (OWASP OAT-005, OAT-021).
controls: Queueing and purchase limits per customer
Bot detection on cart and checkout
Release stock in waves

infrastructure.title: Automation account [name] has broad privileges
infrastructure.desc: RPA and automation bots run with powerful service accounts that are shared, rarely rotated and poorly monitored.
controls: Least-privilege, per-bot accounts
Store bot credentials in a vault
Monitor bot accounts for unusual actions

infrastructure.title: Documents in [name] carry hidden data
infrastructure.desc: Metadata, tracked changes, comments, hidden sheets and "redactions" that are only black boxes reveal information that was meant to be removed.
controls: Strip metadata and hidden content before sharing externally
Use real redaction tools
Export to a flat format for publication

infrastructure.title: Malicious documents opened or parsed by [name] run code
infrastructure.desc: Office files, PDFs and archives exploit macros or flaws in viewers and parsers to run code.
controls: Block macros from the internet; protected view
Convert or sandbox documents from outside (CDR)
Keep viewers and parsing libraries patched
infrastructure.example: Follina (2022, CVE-2022-30190): malicious Word documents ran code through the Windows support diagnostic tool URL handler, even with macros disabled.

infrastructure.title: XML external entities in uploaded documents read files on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Office files (.docx, .xlsx) and SVGs are XML; parsing them with external entities enabled lets an attacker read server files or reach internal URLs.
controls: Disable DTDs and external entities in all XML parsers
Use maintained libraries for office formats
Process uploads in an isolated service

infrastructure.title: Access to sensitive documents in [name] is not tracked
infrastructure.desc: Nobody can tell who viewed, downloaded or shared a document after it leaks.
controls: Enable access and sharing audit logs
Sensitivity labels with logging
Alert on bulk downloads

infrastructure.title: Health records in [name] exposed
infrastructure.desc: Health data is among the most sensitive and valuable data. It is targeted for extortion and protected by special laws (HIPAA, GDPR special categories).
controls: MFA on every remote and administrative access
Encryption and strict role-based access
Network segmentation of clinical systems
infrastructure.example: Change Healthcare (2024): attackers entered through a remote-access portal without MFA, stole health data of about 190 million people and disrupted US claims processing for weeks.

infrastructure.title: Access to patient records in [name] is not logged
infrastructure.desc: Health regulations require that every access is attributable; without it, snooping by staff cannot be detected.
controls: Log every read and change of a record
Break-the-glass access with justification and review
Regular access reviews

infrastructure.title: Outage of [name] stops patient care
infrastructure.desc: Ransomware or a failure makes health records unavailable to clinicians when they need them.
controls: Downtime procedures and read-only copies
Immutable backups with tested restores
Segment clinical systems from office IT

infrastructure.title: Installer or update of [name] replaced with a trojanised version
infrastructure.desc: The build or update server is compromised and ships a signed, malicious version to every customer.
controls: Secure build environment; reproducible builds
Code signing with keys in an HSM
Updates that verify signatures and pin the signing certificate
infrastructure.example: 3CX (2023): the company's signed desktop app installers were trojanised through a supply-chain compromise that itself began with a trojanised third-party application.

infrastructure.title: DLL search-order hijacking when [name] starts
infrastructure.desc: The program loads libraries from its own folder or the working directory, so a planted DLL runs with its rights.
controls: Load libraries by full path; use SetDefaultDllDirectories
Install into protected program folders
Sign and verify loaded modules

infrastructure.title: Unsigned [name] cannot be told apart from a lookalike
infrastructure.desc: Without code signing, users and endpoint protection cannot tell the real program from a malicious copy with the same name and icon.
controls: Sign every executable and installer
Publish checksums
Distribute only through official channels

infrastructure.title: Secrets extracted from [name] by reverse engineering
infrastructure.desc: API keys, passwords and endpoints compiled into the program are easy to extract.
controls: No secrets in client binaries; use per-user tokens
Server-side checks for everything the client is trusted with

infrastructure.title: Company account on [name] taken over
infrastructure.desc: A hijacked company or executive account posts scams, fake announcements or malicious links to people who trust it.
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA on all company social and chat accounts
Managed access (no shared passwords); remove leavers
Monitoring of posts and login alerts
infrastructure.example: Twitter (2020): attackers phone-phished Twitter staff, used an internal admin tool to take over 130 high-profile accounts and posted a bitcoin scam.

infrastructure.title: Confidential data shared on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Staff paste customer data, credentials or plans into chats and channels that include external guests or are kept indefinitely.
controls: Guest and external-sharing policies
DLP and secret scanning on chat platforms
Retention limits

infrastructure.title: Attackers impersonate colleagues or IT support on [name]
infrastructure.desc: External users contact staff on chat platforms pretending to be the help desk or a manager, and talk them into installing remote-access tools or approving MFA prompts.
controls: Restrict who outside the organisation can message staff
Clear labels for external users
Train staff: IT will never ask for this over chat

infrastructure.title: Commitments made on [name] cannot be proven later
infrastructure.desc: Approvals, orders or advice given in chat are lost or deleted, so disputes cannot be resolved.
controls: Use proper systems for approvals
Retention and archiving where required by law
Export important conversations to records

infrastructure.title: Vulnerable plugin in [name] gives remote code execution
infrastructure.desc: CMS plugins and themes are the most common way in: one outdated plugin with a file-upload or injection flaw lets attackers run code on the server.
controls: Install few, well-maintained plugins; remove unused ones
Automatic security updates
Web application firewall with virtual patching
infrastructure.example: WordPress File Manager (2020, CVE-2020-25213): an unauthenticated upload flaw in a plugin installed on about 700,000 sites was mass-exploited before a patch was available.

infrastructure.title: Admin login of [name] brute-forced
infrastructure.desc: Login pages and XML-RPC endpoints are hammered with password guesses.
controls: MFA for all editors and admins
Limit login attempts; disable XML-RPC if unused
Admin area only from known networks or SSO

infrastructure.title: Pages of [name] defaced or injected with spam or skimmers
infrastructure.desc: Attackers with access insert hidden spam links, redirects or card-skimming scripts that run in visitors' browsers.
controls: File-integrity monitoring of themes and plugins
Content Security Policy
Least-privilege editor roles

infrastructure.title: User lists, backups or config files exposed by [name]
infrastructure.desc: Default REST endpoints list user names, and backup or config copies (wp-config.php.bak, database dumps) sit in the web root.
controls: Restrict user-listing endpoints
Keep backups outside the web root
Block access to config and backup file patterns

infrastructure.title: Card skimmer injected into the checkout of [name]
infrastructure.desc: Attackers change a script on the payment page (often a third-party script) and copy card details as customers type them (Magecart).
controls: Content Security Policy and Subresource Integrity on payment pages
Inventory and monitor every script on payment pages (PCI DSS 4.0 req. 6.4.3, 11.6.1)
Use a hosted payment page or iframe from the payment provider
infrastructure.example: British Airways (2018): attackers modified a script on the airline's payment page and captured card details of about 400,000 customers; the UK regulator fined the airline £20 million.

infrastructure.title: Scalper bots buy up stock in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Limited items are bought or reserved by bots within seconds, crowding out customers and overloading checkout.
controls: Purchase limits and queueing
Bot detection on add-to-cart and checkout
Verified accounts for high-demand drops

infrastructure.title: Coupons, gift cards or loyalty points in [name] abused
infrastructure.desc: Discount codes are guessed or reused, gift cards are cracked by enumeration, and loyalty points are stolen or farmed.
controls: Unguessable codes; limit attempts
One-time and per-customer limits enforced on the server
Fraud monitoring on redemptions

infrastructure.title: Customer accounts of [name] taken over to use stored cards and points
infrastructure.desc: Stolen or stuffed credentials give access to saved payment methods, addresses and loyalty balances.
controls: MFA or step-up for purchases with stored cards and address changes
Breached-password checks
Notify customers of new devices and changes

infrastructure.title: Orders in [name] are disputed and there is no proof
infrastructure.desc: Customers claim they did not order or receive goods, and the shop has no authentication or delivery evidence.
controls: Keep authentication results (3-D Secure), IP, device and delivery confirmation per order
Clear order confirmations

infrastructure.title: Fake QR codes stuck over [name] lead to phishing (quishing)
infrastructure.desc: Attackers place their own QR codes on posters, parking meters or emails; the phone opens a convincing fake login or payment page that email filters never saw.
controls: Tamper-evident or digitally displayed codes; regular checks
Show the destination domain clearly before acting
Do not ask for passwords or payments right after a scan

infrastructure.title: Data scanned from [name] is trusted without validation
infrastructure.desc: The content of a QR or barcode is used directly in URLs, queries or commands by the scanning application.
controls: Treat scanned content as untrusted input
Sign QR payloads that carry tickets or identities
Allow-list expected formats

infrastructure.title: QR code [name] contains personal data or tokens in clear
infrastructure.desc: Tickets, health passes and login codes embed data that anyone who photographs the code can read or reuse.
controls: Encode only a random reference, not the data
Short-lived, single-use tokens
Sign codes to prevent forgery

infrastructure.title: Supplier or partner [name] used as a way in
infrastructure.desc: Attackers compromise a vendor with access to your systems and use that trusted connection.
controls: Least-privilege, monitored vendor access
Separate network segment for third-party access
MFA and time-limited accounts for vendors
infrastructure.example: Target (2013): attackers entered with credentials stolen from a refrigeration/HVAC contractor and reached payment systems.

infrastructure.title: [name] receives more data than it needs
infrastructure.desc: Integrations send full records to partners when only a few fields are required, increasing exposure and breaching data-minimisation rules.
controls: Partner-specific APIs/views with only the needed fields
Data processing agreements and periodic review

infrastructure.title: Partner [name] disputes data it sent or received
infrastructure.desc: Without signed messages or delivery receipts, a partner can deny having sent or received an order or file.
controls: Message signing and acknowledgements for B2B exchanges
Keep exchanged messages with timestamps

infrastructure.title: Ransomware encrypts files on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Malware running with a user's or server's rights encrypts everything on mapped shares.
controls: Least-privilege share permissions
Immutable snapshots and offline backups
Detect mass file changes

infrastructure.title: Over-shared folders on [name] ("Everyone" permissions)
infrastructure.desc: Folders are readable by all staff or all authenticated users, exposing HR, finance or customer files.
controls: Review and remove broad permissions
Data-owner approval for access

infrastructure.title: Malicious files planted on [name]
infrastructure.desc: Attackers place infected documents or shortcuts on shared folders that other users open.
controls: Malware scanning on shares
Read-only shares where users only consume content

infrastructure.title: Poisoned pipeline execution in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Pull requests, build scripts or third-party actions run attacker-controlled code inside the pipeline, which has access to secrets and deployment rights.
controls: Do not run untrusted pull requests with secrets
Pin third-party actions to commit SHAs
Separate build and deploy permissions
infrastructure.example: tj-actions/changed-files (2025, CVE-2025-30066): a compromised GitHub Action dumped CI secrets into build logs of thousands of repositories.

infrastructure.title: Secrets in [name] exposed through logs, forks or over-scoped tokens
infrastructure.desc: Pipeline secrets are printed to logs, available to forked builds, or are long-lived tokens with broad scopes.
controls: Short-lived OIDC credentials instead of stored cloud keys
Mask secrets in logs; scope tokens per job
Rotate secrets after incidents
infrastructure.example: CircleCI (2023): malware on an engineer's laptop stole an MFA-backed session; customers had to rotate all secrets stored in the platform.

infrastructure.title: Dependency confusion or typosquatting pulls malicious packages into [name]
infrastructure.desc: Package managers fetch a public package with the same or a similar name as an internal one, running attacker code during the build.
controls: Scoped/namespaced internal packages and a single private registry
Lock files with integrity hashes
Block install scripts where possible
infrastructure.example: Dependency confusion (2021): a researcher got code executed inside dozens of large companies, including Apple and Microsoft, by publishing public packages named like their internal ones.

infrastructure.title: Prompt injection changes what [name] does
infrastructure.desc: Instructions hidden in user input, documents, web pages or emails processed by the model override the system prompt, making it ignore rules, leak data or misuse its tools.
controls: Treat all model input as untrusted; keep instructions and data separate
Least-privilege tools and human approval for impactful actions
Filter and monitor outputs; red-team with injection test sets
