infrastructure.title: [name] reveals sensitive data from prompts, context or training data
infrastructure.desc: The model repeats personal data, secrets or other users' content from its context window, retrieved documents or fine-tuning data.
controls: Do not put secrets in prompts or context
Per-user authorization on retrieved documents (RAG)
Redact personal data before indexing or fine-tuning

infrastructure.title: Excessive agency: [name] takes harmful actions through its tools
infrastructure.desc: An LLM agent can call APIs, run code, send email or change data with broad permissions, so a manipulated or mistaken model acts with those rights.
controls: Give tools the minimum permissions and scope
Require confirmation for state-changing actions
Rate-limit and log every tool call

infrastructure.title: Unbounded model usage makes [name] slow or expensive
infrastructure.desc: Long prompts, large outputs or automated querying consume GPU capacity and paid tokens, causing outages or large bills.
controls: Per-user quotas, input/output token limits and timeouts
Budget alerts on model usage

infrastructure.title: Phishing steals [name]'s credentials or session
infrastructure.desc: Fake login pages — including adversary-in-the-middle kits that relay one-time codes — capture passwords and session cookies.
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys)
Short sessions; bind sessions to device
User reporting of phishing

infrastructure.title: Malware on [name]'s device steals sessions or data
infrastructure.desc: Infostealers and keyloggers on user or administrator devices capture passwords, session cookies and files.
controls: Managed, hardened devices for privileged users
Short sessions bound to device; re-authentication for sensitive actions
Endpoint detection and response
infrastructure.example: LastPass (2022): attackers installed a keylogger on a DevOps engineer's home computer via vulnerable third-party software and used the captured password to reach vault backups.

infrastructure.title: Credential stuffing with passwords leaked elsewhere
infrastructure.desc: Attackers try username/password pairs from other breaches or infostealer logs at scale; reused passwords let them in.
controls: MFA
Breached-password checks
Rate limiting and bot detection on login
infrastructure.example: Snowflake customer accounts (2024): attackers used credentials from infostealer malware against accounts without MFA and stole data from many companies.

infrastructure.title: Shared accounts make actions by [name] untraceable
infrastructure.desc: Several people use the same account, so it is impossible to tell who did what.
controls: Personal accounts only; no shared credentials
Privileged access management with individual check-out

infrastructure.title: Insider misuse of [name]'s legitimate access
infrastructure.desc: Employees, support staff or administrators look up or export data they have access to but no business reason to see.
controls: Least privilege and need-to-know access
Audit and review access to sensitive records
Just-in-time access for support

infrastructure.title: Admin portal [name] reachable from the internet
infrastructure.desc: Administrative interfaces exposed publicly are constantly attacked with stolen credentials and exploits.
controls: Restrict admin access to VPN / zero-trust access or allow-listed networks
Separate admin application from the public site

infrastructure.title: Secrets extracted from the [name] app
infrastructure.desc: API keys, tokens or endpoints embedded in the app binary are recovered by decompiling it.
controls: No long-lived secrets in apps; per-user tokens from the backend
App attestation for backend calls

infrastructure.title: App [name] stores tokens or data insecurely on the device
infrastructure.desc: Tokens and personal data in plain files, shared preferences or logs are readable on rooted devices and in backups.
controls: Use the platform keystore/keychain for secrets
Exclude sensitive data from backups and logs

infrastructure.title: [name] trusts the mobile app to enforce rules
infrastructure.desc: Limits, prices and permissions are only checked in the app, so a modified app or direct API calls bypass them.
controls: Enforce every rule on the server
Treat the app like any other untrusted client

infrastructure.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS) in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Untrusted content is rendered as HTML or script, so attackers run code in other users' browsers with their session.
controls: Context-aware output encoding; framework auto-escaping
Content-Security-Policy
HttpOnly cookies

infrastructure.title: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) against [name]
infrastructure.desc: The browser automatically sends the user's cookies, so a malicious site can make a signed-in user's browser perform actions (change email, transfer money) without their intent.
controls: SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies
Anti-CSRF tokens for state-changing requests
Check the Origin header; never change state on GET

infrastructure.title: Clickjacking against [name]
infrastructure.desc: The site can be framed by another page that tricks users into clicking buttons (approve, delete, transfer) they cannot see.
controls: Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors (or X-Frame-Options)
Confirmation for sensitive actions

infrastructure.title: Price or amount in [name] can be changed by the client
infrastructure.desc: The server trusts price, discount, currency or quantity values sent by the browser or app, so users pay less than they should.
controls: Recalculate amounts server-side from the catalogue/order
Sign or look up amounts when calling the payment provider

infrastructure.title: Card data processed by [name] leaks into logs or storage
infrastructure.desc: Full card numbers or CVV end up in logs, analytics, error reports or the database, bringing the whole system into PCI DSS scope and exposing cardholder data.
controls: Use the payment provider's hosted fields/tokenisation so card data never touches your servers
Mask card numbers in logs; never store CVV

infrastructure.title: Card testing (carding) through [name]
infrastructure.desc: Fraudsters use the checkout to test large numbers of stolen cards with small payments, causing chargebacks, fees and provider sanctions.
controls: Bot detection and rate limits on payment attempts
3-D Secure / risk scoring from the provider
Alert on spikes in declined payments

infrastructure.title: Card data stored in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Storing card numbers (PAN) makes the data store a high-value target and brings it into full PCI DSS scope.
controls: Store payment tokens from the provider instead of card numbers
If unavoidable: strong encryption, key separation, strict access

infrastructure.title: Pre-signed or shared links to [name] leak or live too long
infrastructure.desc: Download links with embedded signatures are shared, logged or cached and keep working for days, giving anyone who has them access to the file.
controls: Short expiry (minutes) for pre-signed URLs
Generate links per user after an authorization check

infrastructure.title: Public write access lets attackers change files in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Anyone can upload or overwrite objects — replacing downloads, scripts or website assets with malicious versions.
controls: Deny public write; only service roles can write
Versioning and object lock for important content

infrastructure.title: Listing enabled on bucket [name]
infrastructure.desc: Anyone allowed to list the bucket can enumerate every object name, then guess or fetch interesting files.
controls: Disable public list permissions
Unguessable object keys for user content

infrastructure.title: Objects in [name] deleted or all versions purged
infrastructure.desc: Without versioning or object lock, a compromised key or mistake permanently deletes data.
controls: Versioning and object lock (WORM) for important data
Separate account for backups; MFA delete

infrastructure.title: [name] exposed to the internet without authentication
infrastructure.desc: Database, search or cache servers that listen on public addresses without authentication are found by scanners within hours and copied or wiped.
controls: Bind to private networks only; firewall rules
Always enable authentication, even internally
Continuous external exposure scanning
infrastructure.example: "Meow" attacks (2020): automated scripts wiped thousands of unsecured Elasticsearch and MongoDB databases.

infrastructure.title: Search results from [name] include documents the user may not see
infrastructure.desc: The search index contains everything, and permissions are not applied when querying, so searches reveal titles and snippets of restricted content.
controls: Filter search results by the user's permissions (document-level security)
Index only what each audience may see

infrastructure.title: Unvalidated document structure corrupts [name]
infrastructure.desc: Schemaless writes accept unexpected fields and types, breaking readers or smuggling data into places it should not be.
controls: Schema validation in the database or the data access layer
Reject unknown fields

infrastructure.title: Event injection into [name]
infrastructure.desc: Functions triggered by queues, storage uploads or webhooks trust event content (file names, metadata, message bodies) that attackers can control.
controls: Validate every event field like user input
Restrict who can publish events or upload files that trigger functions

infrastructure.title: Function [name] hits concurrency limits
infrastructure.desc: Bursts of events use up account-wide concurrency, so this and unrelated functions are throttled.
controls: Reserved concurrency per critical function
Queue and back-pressure in front of functions

infrastructure.title: Attackers run up the cloud or third-party bill of [name]
infrastructure.desc: Autoscaling, serverless functions and paid APIs (SMS, email, AI models) keep serving abusive traffic, turning an attack into a large invoice.
controls: Budgets and billing alerts
Per-user quotas on paid actions (SMS, AI calls)
Caps on autoscaling

infrastructure.title: Missing function-level authorization in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Administrative or privileged functions are reachable by normal users because the check is only done in the UI or not at all.
controls: Deny by default; central authorization for every endpoint
Separate admin APIs and tests that call them as a normal user

infrastructure.title: API responses expose more data than the client needs
infrastructure.desc: Endpoints return full objects (internal IDs, emails, flags, other users' fields) and rely on the front-end to hide them.
controls: Explicit response schemas per endpoint
Never return internal or other users' fields
Review API responses in code review and tests

infrastructure.title: Mass assignment lets users change protected fields
infrastructure.desc: The API binds the whole request body to an object, so a user can set fields they should not control — role, price, owner, verification status.
controls: Explicit allow-lists (DTOs) for writable fields
Separate read and write models
Server-side authorization per field

infrastructure.title: Data from third-party APIs is trusted without validation
infrastructure.desc: Responses from partners or external APIs are used as if they were safe — following their redirects, storing their HTML, passing their values into queries.
controls: Validate and sanitise third-party data like user input
Use TLS and verify certificates for outgoing calls
Timeouts and limits on responses; do not follow redirects blindly

infrastructure.title: Unauthorised producers inject messages into [name]
infrastructure.desc: Any service or host with network access can publish to the queue or topic, so consumers process forged commands or events.
controls: Authentication and per-topic publish permissions
Sign messages that trigger important actions

infrastructure.title: Sensitive messages in [name] readable by many consumers
infrastructure.desc: Topics carry personal or payment data, and any consumer group or administrator can read the whole stream.
controls: Per-topic read permissions; separate topics for sensitive data
Encrypt sensitive payload fields

infrastructure.title: Poison messages crash [name] repeatedly
infrastructure.desc: A malformed or oversized message makes the consumer fail, get redelivered and fail again, blocking all following messages.
controls: Dead-letter queues with retry limits
Schema validation and size limits before processing

infrastructure.title: Logs in [name] contain personal data and are widely accessible
infrastructure.desc: Many engineers, tools and vendors can read logs that include user identifiers, IP addresses or request bodies.
controls: Minimise and pseudonymise logged personal data
Role-based access and retention limits for logs

infrastructure.title: Log flooding hides attacks or overloads [name]
infrastructure.desc: Attackers generate huge volumes of log events so real alerts are lost, storage fills up or the logging budget is exhausted.
controls: Rate-limit and sample noisy events
Alert on sudden log volume changes

infrastructure.title: Audit records in [name] can be rewritten by the people they record
infrastructure.desc: Administrators or the application can update or delete audit and transaction records, so evidence can be removed.
controls: Append-only / write-once storage for audit data
Separate ownership of audit logs from system administration

infrastructure.title: Logs in [name] deleted before incidents are discovered
infrastructure.desc: Short retention means evidence is gone by the time a breach is noticed (often weeks or months later).
controls: Retention long enough for investigations (e.g. 12 months for security logs)
Archive to cheaper immutable storage

infrastructure.title: Database [name] uses default or shared admin credentials
infrastructure.desc: Default, shared or well-known admin passwords give anyone who reaches the database full access.
controls: Unique, vaulted admin credentials; disable default accounts
Individual admin accounts with MFA via a bastion

infrastructure.title: Application connects to [name] with more rights than it needs
infrastructure.desc: The application's database account can change schemas, read every table or act as administrator, so an injection flaw becomes full data compromise.
controls: Separate accounts for migration, application and reporting
Grant only needed tables and operations
No shared admin accounts

infrastructure.title: Expensive queries or lock contention take [name] down
infrastructure.desc: Slow or deliberately heavy queries hold locks and connections so normal requests time out.
controls: Query timeouts and connection pool limits
Indexes for user-driven searches; read replicas
Rate-limit expensive operations

infrastructure.title: Shared database accounts hide who changed [name]
infrastructure.desc: Several applications or people use the same database user, so changes cannot be attributed.
controls: One account per application and per person
Pass end-user identity into audit columns

infrastructure.title: Cache poisoning in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Attackers get malicious or wrong values stored in a cache that other users or services then trust.
controls: Include all relevant inputs in cache keys
Validate data before caching; short TTLs for user-influenced data

infrastructure.title: Sessions or tokens in [name] readable without authentication
infrastructure.desc: Caches inside the network often run without passwords or TLS, so anyone who reaches them can read sessions and cached data.
controls: Enable authentication and TLS on the cache
Network policies limiting access to the application

infrastructure.title: Cache stampede on [name] overloads the backend
infrastructure.desc: When popular entries expire together, many requests hit the database at once.
controls: Request coalescing / locking on refresh
Staggered expiry; serve stale while revalidating

infrastructure.title: One credential can read every secret in [name]
infrastructure.desc: Applications or CI jobs use broad tokens, so compromising one of them exposes all secrets in the store.
controls: Per-application policies limited to their own secrets
Short-lived authentication (workload identity) instead of static tokens

infrastructure.title: Access to secrets in [name] is not audited
infrastructure.desc: Reads and changes of secrets are not logged, so a leaked token's use cannot be traced.
controls: Enable audit devices/logs; alert on unusual reads
Retain secret-access logs centrally

infrastructure.title: Secrets store [name] unavailable stops all services
infrastructure.desc: If the store is down or sealed after a restart, every service that needs a secret fails to start.
controls: High-availability setup and tested unseal procedure
Short-lived caching of secrets in services

infrastructure.title: Secrets in [name] are never rotated
infrastructure.desc: Long-lived credentials stay valid for years, so any past leak is still usable.
controls: Automatic rotation; dynamic short-lived credentials where possible
Alert on secret age

flow.title: Traffic on [name] can be read on the network
flow.desc: The flow is not encrypted and leaves its trust zone, so anyone on the network path can capture credentials and data.
controls: TLS 1.2+ (or mTLS) on every connection
HSTS; disable plaintext fallbacks

flow.title: Traffic on [name] modified in transit (man-in-the-middle)
flow.desc: Without transport encryption and integrity, an attacker on the path can alter requests and responses.
controls: TLS with certificate validation; mTLS between services
Message signing for critical payloads

flow.title: Unauthenticated messages accepted on [name] across a trust boundary
flow.desc: The receiver cannot verify who sent the data, so attackers in the other zone can inject their own requests or messages.
controls: Mutual TLS or signed tokens on the flow
Validate sender identity before processing

flow.title: Sensitive data on [name] sent in cleartext
flow.desc: The flow connects to a component that holds personal data, credentials or other sensitive data, but it is not encrypted.
controls: Encrypt in transit
Send only the fields that are needed

flow.title: Webhook or queue messages on [name] accepted without signature check
flow.desc: Anyone who can reach the endpoint or queue can post fake events (payments, status changes) because messages are not verified.
controls: Verify HMAC signatures or use mTLS
Check timestamps/nonces to reject replays
Restrict who can publish to the queue

flow.title: TLS certificate validation disabled for [name]
flow.desc: Client code skips certificate checks (often to work around test certificates), which silently allows man-in-the-middle attacks.
controls: Never disable verification in production code
Use a private CA for internal certificates
Tests that fail on invalid certificates

flow.title: Captured requests on [name] can be replayed
flow.desc: Requests carry no timestamp, nonce or one-time token, so a captured request (payment, approval) can be sent again.
controls: Nonces/timestamps with short validity
Idempotency keys for one-time actions

flow.title: Tokens or personal data in URLs of [name]
flow.desc: Values in query strings end up in proxy and server logs, browser history and Referer headers.
controls: Send secrets in headers or POST bodies
Referrer-Policy; avoid personal data in URLs

flow.title: Outdated TLS settings on [name] allow downgrade or weak encryption
flow.desc: Old protocol versions and cipher suites allow downgrade attacks and remove forward secrecy, so recorded traffic may be decrypted later.
controls: TLS 1.2+ only (prefer 1.3), ECDHE suites
Regular TLS configuration scans

flow.title: Flooding of [name] from an anonymous source
flow.desc: Anyone can send traffic on this flow into another trust zone, which makes request floods easy.
controls: Rate limiting and DDoS protection at the edge
Patch servers for protocol-level DoS flaws
Autoscaling with limits
flow.example: HTTP/2 Rapid Reset (2023, CVE-2023-44487): rapidly opening and cancelling streams produced record DDoS attacks against major providers.

flow.title: Slow-request attacks hold connections on [name] open (Slowloris)
flow.desc: Clients send requests very slowly to occupy all connection slots on the receiving server.
controls: Header/body timeouts and per-client connection limits
Reverse proxy or load balancer in front

flow.title: [name] depends on a single network path or provider
flow.desc: If the link, DNS, certificate or upstream provider fails, the flow stops and nothing takes over.
controls: Redundant paths/providers for critical flows
Monitor certificate expiry and DNS
Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers

flow.title: WebSocket connection [name] accepted from any website
flow.desc: The server does not check the Origin of WebSocket handshakes, so a malicious page can open a connection with the user's cookies (cross-site WebSocket hijacking).
controls: Validate the Origin header on handshake
Token-based authentication for WebSocket sessions

flow.title: Tokens on [name] leak through redirects, URLs or referrers
flow.desc: Access tokens or authorization codes travel in URL fragments or query strings, where browser history, logs and Referer headers expose them.
controls: Authorization code flow with PKCE; no implicit flow
Tokens in headers or POST bodies; strict Referrer-Policy

flow.title: Email on [name] sent without enforced TLS
flow.desc: Opportunistic STARTTLS can be stripped, so messages travel in plaintext between mail servers.
controls: MTA-STS and TLS reporting
Encrypt sensitive content end-to-end instead of relying on transport

flow.title: Broker connection [name] without TLS or authentication
flow.desc: MQTT, AMQP or Kafka connections run in plaintext or anonymously inside the network, exposing messages and allowing anyone to connect.
controls: TLS and per-client credentials on brokers
Network policies limiting who can reach the broker

flow.title: Administration over [name] uses weak protocols
flow.desc: Telnet, VNC without TLS or legacy RDP settings expose administrator credentials and sessions.
controls: SSH/RDP with modern encryption and network-level authentication
Access only through a bastion or VPN

flow.title: Database connection [name] not encrypted inside the network
flow.desc: Internal database traffic is assumed safe, but anyone on the network path can read queries, results and credentials.
controls: Require TLS on database connections; verify server certificates

flow.title: HTTP request smuggling between proxy and server on [name]
flow.desc: Front-end and back-end servers disagree on where a request ends, letting attackers prepend requests to other users' traffic.
controls: Use HTTP/2 end-to-end or consistent parsing; reject ambiguous requests
Keep proxies and servers updated

flow.title: Missing timeouts on [name] let a slow dependency block callers
flow.desc: Calls without timeouts wait indefinitely, tying up threads and connections until the caller fails too.
controls: Timeouts on every outbound call
Circuit breakers and bulkheads

flow.title: Retry storms on [name] turn a hiccup into an outage
flow.desc: Clients retry immediately and repeatedly, multiplying load on a struggling service.
controls: Exponential backoff with jitter; retry budgets
Honour Retry-After and rate-limit responses

flow.title: Backlog on [name] delays critical events
flow.desc: A slow consumer or a flood of low-priority messages delays important ones (payments, security alerts).
controls: Separate queues/topics by priority
Alert on consumer lag

flow.title: Oversized payloads on [name] exhaust the receiver
flow.desc: Requests or messages without size limits consume memory and CPU when parsed.
controls: Maximum body/message size at gateway and broker
Streaming parsers for large data

flow.title: Replayed webhook events on [name] processed again
flow.desc: A captured, correctly signed event is sent again and triggers the same action twice.
controls: Check signed timestamps and reject old events
Store processed event IDs

flow.title: Secret in the webhook URL for [name] leaks
flow.desc: Webhook URLs with secrets in the path or query end up in logs, tickets and screenshots.
controls: Signature headers instead of secrets in URLs
Rotate webhook secrets

flow.title: Tokens on [name] accepted by the wrong service
flow.desc: A token issued for one API is replayed to another that does not check the audience.
controls: Validate audience (aud) and issuer on every service
Narrow scopes per API

flow.title: LDAP bind on [name] sends passwords in cleartext
flow.desc: Simple binds over plain LDAP expose user and service passwords on the network.
controls: LDAPS or StartTLS required; disable plain simple binds
Use service accounts with minimal rights

flow.title: Phishing links or malicious attachments arrive via [name]
flow.desc: Inbound email is the most common way malware and credential phishing reach users.
controls: Mail filtering, sandboxing and link rewriting
Mark external email; user reporting button

flow.title: Email on [name] auto-forwarded outside the organisation
flow.desc: Attackers with mailbox access create forwarding rules that silently copy mail to them.
controls: Block automatic external forwarding
Alert on new forwarding rules

flow.title: Remote admin session on [name] hijacked
flow.desc: Disconnected or unattended privileged sessions are taken over by another user on the host.
controls: Session time-outs and logoff of disconnected sessions
Restrict who can connect to admin hosts

flow.title: Brute force on [name] locks out administrators
flow.desc: Account lockout policies let attackers lock admins out on purpose during an incident.
controls: Rate limiting and MFA instead of hard lockouts
Admin access only from trusted networks

flow.title: Database credentials for [name] sit in plain connection strings
flow.desc: Connection strings with passwords are stored in config files, environment dumps and logs.
controls: Pull credentials from a secret store; use IAM/managed identities
Never log connection strings

flow.title: Any service can open a connection like [name] to the database
flow.desc: The database port is reachable from many networks, so any compromised host can try to connect.
controls: Network rules allowing only the owning service
Private endpoints

flow.title: Messages on [name] altered at the broker or in transit
flow.desc: Without message-level integrity, anyone with broker access can change events (amounts, statuses) before consumers read them.
controls: Sign critical messages; verify in consumers
Restrict broker admin access

flow.title: Missing security headers on [name] (HSTS, CSP)
flow.desc: Without HSTS the first connection can be downgraded to HTTP; without CSP, injected scripts run freely.
controls: HSTS with preload; Content-Security-Policy
X-Content-Type-Options and frame-ancestors

flow.title: Unvalidated data stored via [name] attacks later readers
flow.desc: What arrives on [name] is stored as-is. Payloads planted now run later, when another component or an administrator reads the data (stored XSS, second-order SQL injection, CSV formula injection).
controls: Validate and normalise on write; encode on output for the context where it is shown
Parameterised queries also for data read back from the store
Prefix or escape cells starting with = + - @ in exports

flow.title: Sensitive data on [name] goes to an external entity
flow.desc: The flow hands sensitive data from your system to a user, partner or device that you do not control. What happens after that — storage, forwarding, retention — is outside your controls.
controls: Send only what the recipient needs; mask or tokenise the rest
Contracts / data-processing agreements for partners
Encrypt the flow and authenticate the recipient

flow.title: Requests on [name] from outside have no size or rate limits
flow.desc: An external entity can send as many or as large requests as it wants across the boundary, so a single client can exhaust the receiver.
controls: Rate limits per client and per IP at the edge
Maximum body, header and upload sizes
Quotas per tenant or API key

flow.title: Internal flow [name] accepts calls from any service on the network
flow.desc: Service-to-service traffic inside the zone is not authenticated, so a single compromised workload can call [name]'s receiver and change data (no zero-trust between services).
controls: Mutual TLS or signed service tokens between services
Authorisation policy per caller (service mesh, API gateway)
Network policies that allow only the expected caller
